courses.name: General Physics II
weekTopics: Faraday's law of induction stated exactly: the emf induced in a closed loop equals minus the time rate of change of the magnetic flux linking it, emf = -N d(Phi)/dt in volts (1 Wb/s = 1 V), a relationship that holds whether the flux changes because the field changes, because the loop moves or deforms, or both - which is why it is called the flux rule.

Faraday's own conclusion that the existence of magnetic flux is not sufficient to produce an induced emf and that the flux must be CHANGING, established by the 1831 magnet-and-ammeter experiment in which the ammeter deflects one way as the magnet approaches, the other way as it recedes, not at all while the magnet is held stationary inside the loop (where the flux is largest of all), and identically when the loop is moved instead of the magnet - so that a coil at rest in the strongest steady field obtainable produces exactly zero volts.

The three and only three ways of changing Phi = B*A*cos(theta) - changing B, changing the enclosed area A, or changing the orientation theta - collected in d(Phi)/dt = A*cos(theta)*(dB/dt) + B*cos(theta)*(dA/dt) - B*A*sin(theta)*(d(theta)/dt), so that relative motion is one cause of induction among several rather than the criterion for it.

Lenz's law as the content of the minus sign: the induced current flows in the sense whose own magnetic field opposes the CHANGE in flux that produced it, so that its field points against the external field when the flux is rising, along the external field when the flux is falling, and does not exist at all when the flux is constant; in pole form, an approaching north pole meets an induced north pole and a receding north pole meets an induced south pole, so that the force always opposes the motion.

The sign convention that gives the minus sign meaning - a chosen positive normal fixes the sign of Phi and, through the right hand, the positive sense of circulation, so that reversing the choice reverses both together and leaves the physical direction of the induced current unchanged - together with the four-step direction algorithm and the energy argument that makes Lenz's law conservation of energy rather than an extra empirical rule.

The two mechanisms by which charges are actually pushed: motional emf B*L*v for a rod with B, L and v mutually perpendicular, derived both from the swept area and from the force q*v x B on the carriers, giving current B*L*v/R, retarding force B^2*L^2*v/R and an exact mechanical-to-electrical power balance (with 0.5*B*L^2*omega for a rod rotating about one end, the 0.5 being the ratio of mean speed to tip speed); and, for a stationary circuit in a changing field, the induced ELECTRIC field of the general form of Faraday's law, the integral of E.dl round a closed path = -d(Phi)/dt, which is non-conservative, exists whether or not a conductor occupies the path, and gives a ring encircling a solenoid an emf although B at the wire is essentially zero - the same induced currents flowing in bulk metal being eddy currents, the basis of magnetic braking and the reason transformer cores are laminated.

courses.name: Elementary Mathematics II (Calculus)
weekTopics: A solid of revolution is produced by revolving a plane region about a line called the axis of revolution, and every volume this week comes from the single formula V = (integral from a to b of A(x) dx), in which A(x) is the area of the cross-section taken perpendicular to the axis at position x and dx is the thickness of one thin slab; the deck's four-step procedure governs every question - sketch the region and identify the axis of revolution (this determines the variable of integration), sketch the cross-section (disc, washer or shell) and choose the matching formula, determine the boundaries of the solid, then set up the definite integral and integrate.

The disc method applies when the axis of revolution is itself a boundary of the region, so that each perpendicular cross-section is a full circle: V = pi * (integral from a to b of [f(x)]^2 dx) about the x-axis, and V = pi * (integral from c to d of [g(y)]^2 dy) about the y-axis with x = g(y).

The washer method applies when a gap separates the region from the axis, so each cross-section is an annulus and V = pi * (integral from a to b of ([R(x)]^2 - [r(x)]^2) dx), where R is the distance from the axis to the far boundary and r the distance to the near boundary; the squares are taken before the subtraction, because pi*(R^2 - r^2) is a difference of areas and is not pi*(R - r)^2.

The shell method slices parallel to the axis instead of perpendicular to it: a tube of radius x, height h(x) and thickness dx unrolls into a slab 2*pi*x by h(x) by dx, giving V = 2*pi*(integral from a to b of x*h(x) dx) about the y-axis and V = 2*pi*(integral from c to d of y*h(y) dy) about the x-axis, and it is the only practical route when the boundary curve cannot be inverted.

The axis of revolution together with the direction of slicing fixes the variable of integration, and the two families take opposite variables: discs and washers stack along the axis (dx about the x-axis or y = k, dy about the y-axis or x = h) while shells stack across it (dy about the x-axis or y = k, dx about the y-axis or x = h).

Rotating about a line y = k or x = h changes only the radius and never the formula, because a radius is always a distance from the axis: R = |f(x) - k| about y = k and R = |x - h| about x = h, and the region must lie entirely on one side of the axis, since a region that straddles it sweeps the two halves into the same solid; whichever method is used, the other one - when it can be set up - is an exact check on it.

courses.name: Introduction to Problem Solving
weekTopics: Modularisation is defined as the process of dividing a program's functionality into independent modules, such that each independent module has everything it needs to implement only a part of the program's functionality - two clauses which are, respectively, the demand for low coupling and the demand for high cohesion - and decomposition is the same act named from the other side, since by separating the codes in an application into different modules and functions we are essentially decomposing the application into modules.

The course's argument for decomposing is about change rather than length: in a function of more than five thousand lines, changing a part of the code can affect other parts of the code, and modularisation is what ensures that changes can be made to different parts of the code without affecting other parts and that new functionality can be added in a quick and flexible manner; its five stated advantages are that large programs can be written by several or different people, that smaller modules and functions are easier to manage and add, that a small module or function is easier to understand, that modules and functions are easily reused in this program or in another, and that smaller units are easier and faster to design, develop, test and publish, while its five stated disadvantages - longer execution time, increased storage size, longer compilation and loading time, increased inter-module communication problems, and more initial design time - are the price of those advantages rather than symptoms of bad design.

Module independence is governed by the single responsibility principle, which demands that modules should not have more than a single responsibility and should not depend on other modules, and it is measured by two separate readings taken in two different places: cohesion, the extent to which the functions in a module work together to achieve the ultimate aim of the module, taken inside one module and wanted high; and coupling, the extent to which modules depend on other modules before performing their function, taken across a boundary and wanted low - so that neither is judged by the number of calls, and the car analogy of steering wheel, radiator, battery and brake shows a real dependency running through a narrow interface rather than the absence of dependency.

Information hiding requires that modules be specified and designed so that the data structures and processing details of one module are not accessible to other modules, and that they pass only that much information to each other as is required to accomplish the software functions; its three stated benefits are that it emphasises communication through controlled interfaces, decreases the probability of adverse effects, and restricts the effects of changes in one component on others - which makes it the mechanism that produces low coupling, since a module can only depend on what it is able to reach.

Refactoring is a process of modifying a software system to improve the internal structure of design without changing its external behaviour, reducing the complexity of module design while keeping its behaviour or function unchanged, and the deck's worked case is a cohesion repair in which a component performing four functions with a limited relationship with one another is split into four components each exhibiting high cohesion, leading to easier integration, testing and maintenance; structural partitioning of a hierarchical design is either horizontal, in which control modules communicate between functions and execute them at the cost of passing more data across the module interface and a more complex control flow, or vertical, in which functionality is distributed top-down with control modules deciding and doing little processing and worker modules performing all input, computation and output.

Software architecture is the structure of the system, containing the various components of a program or system, the attributes or properties of those components and the relationship between them, and it is needed because it enables efficient communication between stakeholders, highlights early design decisions affecting coding and testing, and creates intellectual models of how the system is organised and how its components interact; software patterns describe reusable solutions to recurring design problems at three levels - architectural patterns (high-level, often considered equivalent to software architecture), design patterns (medium-level, refining the elements an architectural pattern defines and often considered equivalent to software components) and idioms (low-level, programming-language specific, often termed coding patterns) - and the two generic design approaches are top-down, which decomposes the whole system repeatedly and suits a solution designed from scratch whose specific details are unknown, and bottom-up, which composes higher-level components from basic primitives with abstraction increasing at each level and suits a system built from an existing one, neither being individually practicable so that a good combination of both is used.

courses.name: General Physics Practical II
weekTopics: Experiment to determine the magnitude of the magnetic permeability of free space, mu_0, by mapping the magnetic flux density along the axis of a circular current-carrying loop using a loop of known radius R, a DC power supply, an ammeter, a movable magnetic probe and a Tesla meter, the historical premise being Oersted's 1820 observation that a compass needle near a current-carrying conductor deflects by an amount that grows with the current; the routine is to select Coil 1 (R = 0.10 m), set I = 1 A, place the probe at z = 0, click Record, then step the probe out along the axis in 2 cm intervals for 20 readings in all (z = 0 to 38 cm), repeat for coils of different radius, and download the Excel sheet.

The axial field of a single circular loop, B(z) = mu_0*I*R^2 / [2*(R^2 + z^2)^(3/2)], derived from Biot-Savart by noting that dl is perpendicular to r everywhere on the axis (so sin(theta) = 1), that the off-axis components cancel by symmetry leaving the axial component dB*(R/r), and that the integral of dl round the loop is 2*pi*R; here B(z) is in tesla, I in amperes, R and z in metres, and mu_0 = 4*pi*10^-7 H/m = 4*pi*10^-7 T*m/A, with the whole expression multiplied by N for N turns.

The special cases and behaviour of that field: B is a maximum at the centre where it reduces to B_0 = mu_0*I/(2R), giving 6.28 x 10^-6 T = 6283 nT for the deck's coil (R = 0.10 m, I = 1 A) against a measured 6285 nT; it falls to half its central value at z = 0.766*R; and for z >> R it tends to the point-dipole form mu_0*I*R^2/(2*z^3), which is already 11 per cent too high at z = 38 cm for this coil, so the full formula must be used throughout.

The linearisation and the analysis: because B is not linear in z, compute for every recorded row the factor x = I*R^2 / [2*(R^2 + z^2)^(3/2)], which is numerically the magnetic field strength H in A/m, then plot B in tesla against x to obtain a straight line through the origin of gradient mu_0, in units T/(A/m) = T*m/A = H/m; the intercept must be zero, and a non-zero intercept means the Tesla meter was not zeroed against the Earth's field, which at about 50 microtesla is roughly eight times the loop's own central field.

Permeability as a general quantity, and the experiment's error budget: mu = B/H is the permeability of a medium in H/m, mu = mu_r * mu_0 where mu_r = mu/mu_0 is the dimensionless relative permeability (about 1 for air and vacuum, which is why the experiment performed in air measures mu_0, and in the hundreds or thousands for ferromagnets), not to be confused with susceptibility chi = mu_r - 1, with the electric analogue epsilon_0 = 8.85 x 10^-12 F/m, or with the field quantities B (tesla), H (A/m) and flux Phi (weber); the deck lists no precautions, so the standard set applies - zero the Tesla meter, keep the probe on the axis with its sensitive direction along the axis, measure z from the plane of the loop and R to the mean radius of the winding, watch the current for thermal drift, clear iron from the bench, and convert nT to T and cm to m before computing anything.

courses.name: Nigerian Peoples and Culture
weekTopics: The "Makers of Nigeria": nine Nigerians drawn from politics, the economy and the creative industry whose contributions to national development and to the journey to independence the lesson asks you to identify, examine and account for.

The nationalist politicians: Herbert Macaulay (1864-1946), tagged the father of Nigerian nationalism, who protested colonial policy on water rates, land and railway finances in the 1920s and founded the Nigerian National Democratic Party in 1923 as Nigeria's first political party; Obafemi Awolowo (1909-1987), first premier of the western region from 1954 to 1960, leader of the Action Group and campaigner for the federal constitution introduced in the 1954 Lyttelton Constitution; and Nnamdi Azikiwe (1904-1996), last governor-general from 1960 to 1963, first elected president from 1963 to 1966, co-founder of the NCNC and inspiration of the Zikist movement.

Funmilayo Ransome-Kuti (1900-1978), the "Lioness of Lisabi", who mobilised market women and organised resistance to colonial rule, whose 1953 Abeokuta conference on women's welfare produced the Federation of Nigerian Women's Societies, and who died on 13 April 1978 of injuries sustained when soldiers raided her son Fela's Lagos residence on 18 February 1977.

The creative and cultural figures: Fela Anikulapo-Kuti (1938-1997), credited with creating Afrobeat in the early 1970s and with changing the relationship between music and Nigerian socio-political discourse; Chinua Achebe (1930-2013), author of Things Fall Apart (1958), head of the Biafra Broadcasting Service and PRP deputy national vice president in 1983; and Wole Soyinka (1934-present), imprisoned for 22 months in 1967, exiled in 1994, and the first African to win the Nobel Prize for Literature, in 1986.

Gani Fawehinmi (1938-2009), "the people's lawyer", who practised in Lagos from 1965, campaigned for human rights for 40 years through repeated detentions and the burning of his library, and pressed the unsolved 1986 parcel-bomb killing of the editor Dele Giwa; and Nwankwo Kanu (1976-present), whose contribution won Nigeria the 1996 Olympic Gold past Brazil and Argentina and who serves as a UNICEF ambassador funding care for Nigerian children with heart complications.

From the Summary PDF only: the contribution of the Nigerian diaspora to national development, its historical roots in pre-modern migration, the slave trade and contemporary economic migration, remittances as a source of foreign exchange and a contributor to GDP, the achievements of Nigerians in the United States, and the strategies needed to harness diaspora potential while addressing criminality among a minority.

courses.name: Communication in English II
weekTopics: Hearing versus listening: hearing is a passive and involuntary physiological event, whereas listening is an active and voluntary process requiring a conscious effort to interpret and understand spoken messages.

The six headings under which the deck sets out the importance of listening - Effective Communication, Building Relationships, Conflict Resolution, Learning and Growth, Leadership Effectiveness, and Avoiding Miscommunication - each with its own stated benefits and consequences.

Active listening techniques named in the learning objectives and case study: paraphrasing, summarising, asking clarifying questions, note-taking, minimising distractions, avoiding prejudgment, plus nonverbal communication and empathetic listening.

Listening for academic success: effective listening as the basis for understanding course content, following instructions and grasping complex concepts, especially in subjects requiring comprehension of intricate detail from lectures and discussions.

Cultural awareness and reflective practice as listening skills: recognising and respecting communication differences across cultures, and using regular self-assessment to identify areas for improvement in one's own listening.

courses.name: Introduction to Web Technologies
weekTopics: Web application security is the practice of protecting web applications from threats that compromise the confidentiality, integrity or availability of data, and the week separates a vulnerability (a weakness in an application's design, implementation or configuration) from a threat (a potential danger such as SQL injection, cross-site scripting or DDoS).

The five named web application vulnerabilities are SQL injection (malicious SQL inserted into user inputs, e.g. entering ' OR 1=1-- in a login form), cross-site scripting (malicious scripts injected into pages viewed by other users, causing data theft or session hijacking), cross-site request forgery (tricking an authenticated user into an unwanted action without consent), other injection attacks such as command injection and XML injection, and security misconfigurations such as database credentials left in plaintext configuration files.

The seven security best practices each answer a specific vulnerability (input validation with parameterised queries against injection, output encoding with a Content Security Policy against XSS, strong authentication and role-based authorisation with two-factor authentication, secure session management with unique tokens against CSRF, security headers such as HSTS and X-Content-Type-Options, regular updates, and security testing through vulnerability scanning, penetration testing and code reviews), and they are reinforced at runtime by a Web Application Firewall that filters and monitors HTTP/HTTPS requests, inspecting incoming traffic for malicious patterns or payloads and blocking threats before they reach the application, and at development time by secure coding without hard-coded credentials, regular code review, and DevSecOps that builds security into the DevOps pipeline rather than leaving it as an afterthought.

Server deployment (setting up and configuring servers through hardware setup, software installation and network configuration) and hosting (providing server resources so an application is reachable on the internet) come in four options: on-premises for complete control at high maintenance cost, cloud hosting on AWS, Azure or GCP for scalability, flexibility and cost-efficiency, virtual private servers such as DigitalOcean for a balance of control and cost, and shared hosting such as Bluehost for the lowest cost with performance and customisation limits.

Scalability and performance optimisation cover horizontal scaling (adding more machines or instances, usually behind a load balancer such as NGINX or AWS Elastic Load Balancing) versus vertical scaling (upgrading the existing server's CPU, memory or storage), together with caching, content delivery networks such as Cloudflare, database indexing and front-end optimisation through minification and lazy loading.

Monitoring is the continuous real-time observation of an application's performance, health and behaviour through metrics, alerts and logging, debugging is the identification and resolution of code defects through error handling, debugging tools such as Chrome DevTools and version control with Git, and continuous integration automatically builds, tests and deploys code changes as they are committed to version control using tools such as Jenkins and Travis CI.

checks.topic: Volumes of solids of revolution as concepts: what the disc, washer and shell methods each are and where their integrands come from, what feature of the geometry forces one rather than another, why a washer subtracts areas and not radii, how the axis of revolution together with the direction of slicing fixes the variable of integration, and how rotating about y = k or x = h changes the radius without changing the formula.

questions.q: The formula V = pi * (integral from a to b of [f(x)]^2 dx) is obtained by arguing that:
options: the region has area (integral from a to b of f(x) dx) and it is swept through 2*pi radians, so the volume is 2*pi times that area
a plane cut perpendicular to the x-axis meets the solid in a circle of radius f(x), whose area is pi*[f(x)]^2; a slab of thickness dx therefore has volume pi*[f(x)]^2 dx
the area (integral from a to b of f(x) dx) is squared and multiplied by pi, since a circle's area is pi times a squared length
the strip at x has area f(x) dx and travels a distance 2*pi*x as it revolves, so its swept volume is 2*pi*x*f(x) dx
questions.concept: A solid of revolution is integrated by slicing it perpendicular to its axis; the integrand is the area of one slice.
questions.why: Every point of the region at abscissa x has been carried right round the axis, so the plane cut at x is a full circle of radius f(x); its area is pi*[f(x)]^2 and the slab of thickness dx contributes pi*[f(x)]^2 dx. (a) is the 'swept through 2*pi radians' argument, which would give 2*pi*(integral of f dx) - an area times an angle, not a volume, and for y = sqrt(x) on [0, 4] it gives 32*pi/3 instead of 8*pi. (c) squares after integrating instead of before, and pi*[(integral of f dx)]^2 != pi*(integral of f^2 dx); for the same example it gives pi*(16/3)^2 = 256*pi/9. (d) is the SHELL integrand, correct for revolution about the y-axis and wrong here, because the strip at x is parallel to the x-axis's own direction and does not travel a distance 2*pi*x about it.

questions.q: In exactly one of the following, the cross-sections perpendicular to the axis of revolution are DISCS rather than washers. Which?
options: the region between y = x and y = x^2 on [0, 1], revolved about the x-axis
the region under y = sqrt(x) on [0, 4] (above the x-axis), revolved about the x-axis
the region bounded by y = x^2, y = 0 and x = 2, revolved about the y-axis
the region bounded by y = x^2, y = 0, x = 0 and x = 2, revolved about the line y = -1
questions.concept: Cross-sections are discs precisely when the axis of revolution is a boundary of the region, so no hole is punched.
questions.why: Under y = sqrt(x) the region reaches down to y = 0 at every x in (0, 4], so the cut at x is a solid circle of radius sqrt(x). (a) has two curves that meet only at the endpoints x = 0 and x = 1; strictly between them the region is bounded below by y = x^2 > 0, so every interior cut is a washer of hole radius x^2 - touching the axis at isolated points does not close the hole. (c) kills the popular rule 'one curve means disc': there is one curve, but the axis is VERTICAL, and the horizontal cut at height y runs from x = sqrt(y) out to x = 2, a washer with inner radius sqrt(y). (d) has a gap of exactly 1 between the region's lowest edge y = 0 and the axis y = -1, so every cut is a washer with inner radius 1. The criterion is never 'how many curves' - it is whether the region touches the axis all along the interval.

questions.q: The deck's first step says that identifying the axis of revolution 'determines the variable of integration'. Stated precisely, this is because:
options: the variable is the one the axis is named after - an x-axis rotation is integrated in x, a y-axis rotation in y
the slices must always be taken perpendicular to the axis, and the variable of integration measures position along the axis

the slice thickness lies in a direction fixed jointly by the axis and by whether the slices are perpendicular or parallel to it, and the variable of integration is the coordinate measured in that direction
the variable is whichever one the boundary curve has already been written in terms of
questions.concept: The variable of integration is the direction in which the slices are stacked, and that depends on the axis and on the slicing direction together.
questions.why: Disc and washer slices are perpendicular to the axis, so they stack along it: about a horizontal axis, dx; about a vertical axis, dy. Shell slices are parallel to the axis, so they stack across it: about a vertical axis, dx; about a horizontal axis, dy. (a) is true for discs and washers only and is exactly backwards for shells - it is the reason students write 2*pi*(integral of y*(...) dy) for a rotation about the y-axis. (b) states the perpendicular rule as though it were universal, which quietly outlaws the shell method. (d) is the refusal to invert: how a curve happens to be written is a fact about the page, not about the solid, and a washer about the y-axis requires x = g(y) whether or not you were given it that way.

questions.q: In the shell integrand 2*pi*x*h(x) dx, the factor 2*pi*x is there because:
options: 2*pi*x is the area of the circle of radius x that the strip sweeps out
the shell of radius x, height h(x) and thickness dx can be slit and unrolled into a slab of dimensions 2*pi*x by h(x) by dx, so 2*pi*x is its length
the strip has two ends, each contributing a circle of circumference pi*x
a full revolution is 2*pi radians, so every volume of revolution carries a factor 2*pi
questions.concept: A shell is a thin tube; unrolled, it is a rectangular slab whose length is the circumference at its radius.
questions.why: Slitting the tube of radius x, height h and thickness dx and flattening it gives dimensions 2*pi*x (circumference) by h (height) by dx (thickness), so dV = 2*pi*x*h*dx. Exactly, the tube is pi*(x + dx)^2*h - pi*x^2*h = pi*h*(2*x*dx + dx^2), and the dx^2 term is negligible in the limit, so the finished integral is not an approximation. (a) confuses circumference with area: the area of the circle of radius x is pi*x^2, and using it would give a solid cylinder rather than a tube. (c) invents a geometry - the two ends of a shell are annuli of negligible area, and pi*x is not a circumference anyway. (d) is the same '2*pi radians' error as in question 1; the 2*pi here is a LENGTH, which is why it multiplies a radius that varies from strip to strip instead of being pulled out as a constant angle.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = f(x) (with f(x) > 0 throughout), the x-axis, x = a and x = b is revolved about the line y = -2. The correct radii are:
options: R = f(x), r = 0
questions.concept: The radius is the distance from the axis to the boundary, so it is (boundary coordinate) minus (axis coordinate).
questions.why: With the axis at y = -2, the far boundary y = f(x) is at distance f(x) - (-2) = f(x) + 2, and the near boundary y = 0 is at distance 0 - (-2) = 2. (a) ignores the shift entirely and computes the solid about y = 0, a completely different solid. (c) writes f(x) - 2 by subtracting the MAGNITUDE of k instead of k itself - the sign of k is the whole point - and it also produces the absurd negative inner radius -2. (d) is the half-correction that is by far the most common: the outer radius is shifted correctly, but the student forgets that the shift has opened a cylindrical hole of radius 2 down the middle, and so adds a solid core that is not part of the solid.

questions.q: A washer's cross-sectional area is pi*(R^2 - r^2) and not pi*(R - r)^2 because:
options: pi*(R - r)^2 would be negative whenever r > R
R^2 - r^2 = (R - r)(R + r), so the two expressions are equal and either may be used
pi*(R - r)^2 is the area of a circle whose radius is the washer's WIDTH, which is a different region; the annulus is the outer disc with the inner disc removed, so its area is pi*R^2 - pi*r^2
R and r are functions of x, and the square of a difference of two functions is not defined
questions.concept: The washer is a difference of two discs, so its area is a difference of two areas.
questions.why: Remove the disc of radius r from the disc of radius R: pi*R^2 - pi*r^2 = pi*(R^2 - r^2). (a) is irrelevant - a square is never negative, and in a correctly set up washer R >= r anyway. (b) is the near-miss that catches the most people: R^2 - r^2 does factor, but as (R - r)(R + r), NOT as (R - r)^2; the two agree only when R + r = R - r, i.e. r = 0, which is precisely the disc case where there is no hole to argue about. (d) is fabricated: (f - g)^2 is perfectly well defined; it simply computes the area of a circle whose radius is the gap, which is not the shape the slice has.

questions.q: A region lying above the x-axis between x = a and x = b, with 0 < a < b, is to be revolved about the y-axis. The correct pairing of method with variable is:
options: washers in dx, shells in dy
washers in dy, shells in dx
both in dx, since the region's boundaries are given as functions of x
both in dy, since the axis of revolution is the y-axis
questions.concept: Perpendicular slices stack along the axis, parallel slices stack across it, so the two families take opposite variables.
questions.why: About the y-axis a washer is a horizontal annulus at height y whose radii are x-values, so the stacking direction is y and the integral is pi*(integral of (R(y)^2 - r(y)^2) dy); a shell is a vertical tube at abscissa x, so the stacking direction is x and the integral is 2*pi*(integral of x*h(x) dx). (a) is the exact swap, and it is what produces the notorious '2*pi*(integral of y*(...) dy) about the y-axis'. (c) lets the notation of the question dictate the variable and so refuses to invert the curve, which makes the washer integral unwritable. (d) applies the disc/washer rule to both families, which would forbid the shell method's single greatest advantage - that it needs no inversion.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = 2x^2 - x^3 and the x-axis (0 <= x <= 2) is revolved about the y-axis, and the shell method is the only practical route. The reason is:
options: a cubic cannot be integrated, so no method requiring (integral of (2x^2 - x^3) dx) can be used
a washer setup about a vertical axis needs both boundaries written as x = (function of y), and y = 2x^2 - x^3 cannot be solved for x
the region touches the y-axis at the origin, so the inner radius of a washer would be zero
whenever the axis of revolution is the y-axis, shells must be used
questions.concept: Discs and washers about a vertical axis need the boundaries as functions of y; shells about a vertical axis need them as functions of x.
questions.why: The washer at height y would require the two x-values on the curve at that height, i.e. the roots of x^3 - 2x^2 + y = 0 - a cubic in x with no usable closed form, and in fact two branches. Shells need only y = 2x^2 - x^3 as given, with radius x and height 2x^2 - x^3. (a) is false and confuses two different operations: (integral of (2x^2 - x^3) dx) is elementary; what cannot be done is INVERTING the relation. (c) inverts the logic - an inner radius of zero is not an obstacle, it is exactly the condition that makes a washer degenerate into a disc, which is easier, not harder. (d) is a blanket rule that is simply untrue: worked from y-boundaries, x = sqrt(y) about the y-axis is a routine disc problem.

questions.q: Every method this week is a special case of V = (integral from a to b of A(x) dx). State what A(x) is, what has to be true of the slices for the formula to hold, and show how the disc and the washer are both instances of it. Then explain why a cylindrical shell is NOT a cross-section of the solid, and why the shell method is nevertheless exact.
questions.concept: All three methods are the single formula V = (integral of A(x) dx) applied to different decompositions; the disc and washer supply cross-sectional areas, while the shell supplies a nested-tube decomposition that is exact in the limit.
questions.why: If a solid lies between the planes x = a and x = b, and A(x) denotes the AREA OF THE PLANE CROSS-SECTION AT x TAKEN PERPENDICULAR TO THE x-AXIS, then a slab between x and x + dx has volume approximately A(x) dx, and summing and taking the limit gives V = (integral from a to b of A(x) dx). The requirement is only that A(x) be a genuine cross-sectional area and vary continuously, so that the slab's volume is A(x) dx to first order. For a solid of revolution about the x-axis every cross-section is a circle or an annulus, because the region has been carried right round the axis: if the region reaches the axis, A(x) = pi*[f(x)]^2, which is the DISC method; if it does not, the same cut has a concentric hole of radius r(x), so A(x) = pi*([R(x)]^2 - [r(x)]^2), which is the WASHER method. The two are one formula with r = 0 or r != 0. A cylindrical shell is different in kind: it is not a plane cut of the solid at all, but one of a family of NESTED TUBES filling the solid from the axis outwards, so its thickness dx is measured radially, across the axis rather than along it. It is still exact, because the tube of radius x, height h(x) and thickness dx has volume pi*(x + dx)^2*h - pi*x^2*h = 2*pi*x*h*dx + pi*h*dx^2, and the dx^2 term contributes nothing in the limit; the sum of the tubes is therefore (integral of 2*pi*x*h(x) dx). Both decompositions fill the same solid without overlap, so both must give the same number - which is why one is the best available check on the other.

questions.q: A student computes the volume generated by revolving the region between y = x and y = x^2 on [0, 1] about the x-axis as pi*(integral from 0 to 1 of (x - x^2)^2 dx). Identify the error precisely, evaluate both that integral and the correct one, and say what solid, if any, the student's number describes.
questions.concept: A washer's integrand is a difference of areas, pi*(R^2 - r^2), and (R - r)^2 is not R^2 - r^2.
questions.why: The error is squaring the DIFFERENCE OF THE RADII instead of differencing the SQUARES. The strip at x runs from y = x^2 up to y = x, and when it is revolved about the x-axis it sweeps an annulus whose outer radius is R = x (distance from the axis to the upper curve) and whose inner radius is r = x^2 - so its area is pi*(x^2 - x^4), not pi*(x - x^2)^2. Correct: V = pi*(integral from 0 to 1 of (x^2 - x^4) dx) = pi*[x^3/3 - x^5/5] from 0 to 1 = pi*(1/3 - 1/5) = 2*pi/15, about 0.419. The student's: pi*(integral from 0 to 1 of (x^2 - 2x^3 + x^4) dx) = pi*(1/3 - 1/2 + 1/5) = pi*(10 - 15 + 6)/30 = pi/30, about 0.105. The two are not related by any constant, and the student's is far too small - as it must be, since (R - r)^2 < R^2 - r^2 whenever 0 < r < R. Geometrically, pi*(x - x^2)^2 is the area of a CIRCLE WHOSE RADIUS IS THE WIDTH OF THE GAP between the curves, so the student's number is the volume of a solid whose cross-section at x is a small disc of radius x - x^2, a shape with no relation to the annulus actually produced. The tell is that the answer does not depend on how far the region sits from the axis: shift both curves up by 5 and pi*(R - r)^2 is unchanged, while the true volume grows enormously.

questions.q: Explain why the radius in every one of these formulas is a distance from the axis, and use that to write down the outer radius for a curve y = f(x) > 0 revolved about (i) the x-axis, (ii) the line y = k with k < 0, and (iii) the line x = h with the region entirely to the left of it. Then say what goes wrong if the region straddles the axis of revolution, and what you do instead.
questions.concept: A radius is a distance from the axis of revolution, so it is always (coordinate of the boundary) minus (coordinate of the axis), taken so as to be non-negative.
questions.why: When a point is revolved about a line, the circle it traces has radius equal to its perpendicular distance from that line - this is the only geometric fact behind every formula this week, and it is why the formulas themselves never change when the axis moves. Hence: (i) about the x-axis (y = 0), R = f(x) - 0 = f(x); (ii) about y = k with k < 0, R = f(x) - k = f(x) + |k|, and the region no longer touches the axis, so an inner radius r = 0 - k = |k| appears and the problem becomes a washer; (iii) about the vertical line x = h with the region entirely to the left, every point has x <= h, so the distance is h - x, and writing x - h instead makes every radius negative and the final volume negative. If the region STRADDLES the axis - part of it on each side - the two parts sweep into the SAME space, and adding their contributions counts the overlap twice. The correct treatment is to revolve only the part that is further from the axis on each cut, i.e. to take R as the largest distance and r as the smallest distance achieved on that side; in the common symmetric case (a region symmetric about the axis, such as -1 <= y <= 1 revolved about y = 0) the solid generated is exactly the one generated by either half, so you integrate one half only and do NOT double it. Reporting twice the volume because 'there are two halves' is the standard casualty here.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = x^2, y = 0 and x = 2 can be revolved about the y-axis by washers or by shells. Explain what the slices look like in each case, which variable each forces, and exactly what work each method demands of you before the integral can even be written. Do not evaluate either integral.
questions.concept: The two families slice the same solid in perpendicular directions, so they force opposite variables and impose opposite demands on how the boundary curves must be written.
questions.why: The region is bounded above by y = x^2, below by y = 0, and on the right by x = 2; the axis is the y-axis. WASHERS: the slices are perpendicular to the axis, so they are horizontal annuli at height y, and they stack in the y-direction - the variable is dy and the limits are y-values, from y = 0 to y = 4 (the height of the corner (2, 4)). At height y the solid runs from the parabola out to the line x = 2, so the inner radius is the parabola expressed as x = sqrt(y) and the outer radius is the constant 2, giving pi*(integral from 0 to 4 of (2^2 - (sqrt(y))^2) dy). The work demanded BEFORE integrating is therefore inverting the curve (y = x^2 -> x = sqrt(y)), converting the corner point into a y-limit, and recognising that the parabola supplies the INNER radius since it lies nearer the axis. SHELLS: the slices are parallel to the axis, so they are vertical tubes at abscissa x, and they stack in the x-direction - the variable is dx and the limits are x-values, from x = 0 to x = 2. The tube at x has radius x (its distance from the y-axis) and height (top minus bottom) = x^2 - 0, giving 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of x*x^2 dx). Here nothing needs inverting, since the curve is already y = f(x), but you must identify the radius as the DISTANCE x rather than the function value, and the height as a Week 10 'top minus bottom' rather than simply the upper curve. The two integrals look nothing alike and are in different variables; both are exact, and their agreement is the check.

checks.topic: Faraday's and Lenz's laws as concepts: the exact statement of Faraday's law and why it is the RATE of change of flux linkage that induces, what each of the four observations of the 1831 magnet-and-ammeter experiment separately proves, what the minus sign in emf = -N d(Phi)/dt is doing and how the positive normal, the sign of Phi and the positive sense of circulation are tied together by the right hand, Lenz's law as conservation of energy rather than an extra empirical rule, the four-step procedure for finding the direction of the induced current in named geometries, and motional emf derived both from the swept area and from the force q*v x B on the carriers.

questions.q: In Faraday's experiment the ammeter deflects when the MAGNET is moved towards the loop, and deflects in exactly the same way when the LOOP is moved towards the magnet. This shows that:
options: only the RELATIVE motion matters, because either version changes the flux through the loop at the same rate
the magnet drags its field along with it, so a moving magnet and a moving loop are physically the same event
two different laws are at work in the two cases, and it is a coincidence that they give the same reading
the two deflections agree only if the two speeds are equal, which the experimenter must arrange
questions.concept: Faraday's law depends on d(Phi)/dt, and only relative motion changes it
questions.why: The loop has no way of telling which body is moving; it responds only to the rate at which the flux threading it changes, and equal relative speeds give equal d(Phi)/dt and equal emf. Option (b) invents a mechanism - a field is not a substance carried along. Option (c) is the subtlest error: the microscopic mechanisms do differ (a moving rod has its carriers pushed by q*v x B, a stationary loop in a changing field by an induced electric field), but the agreement is not a coincidence - the flux rule emf = -d(Phi)/dt covers both as one law, and that consistency is the observation Einstein opened special relativity with. Option (d) confuses a controlled comparison with a physical requirement: the character of the deflection is the same at any speed.

questions.q: You take the positive normal of a loop to point OUT of the page, then change your mind and take it INTO the page instead. As a result:
options: the sign of Phi reverses, the positive sense of circulation reverses with it, and the PHYSICAL direction of the induced current is unchanged
the sign of Phi reverses, so the induced current now flows the opposite way round the loop
nothing at all changes, since Phi = B*A*cos(theta) is a magnitude and has no sign
Faraday's law acquires a plus sign, since the minus sign is there only for the standard choice of normal
questions.concept: The sign convention is a bookkeeping choice; Lenz's law is not
questions.why: The positive normal fixes both the sign of Phi and, through the right hand, which way round the loop counts as positive circulation; reverse it and both flip together, so emf = -d(Phi)/dt returns the current in the same physical place. Option (b) flips one half of the convention and not the other - the error of a student who gets a negative answer and reverses the current on that basis alone. Option (c) is wrong on the definition: Phi = B.A is a SIGNED scalar, which is exactly why a coil flipped through 180 degrees registers d(Phi) = 2*B*A rather than zero. Option (d) misplaces the minus sign, which encodes Lenz's law - a physical fact - and does not depend on the normal chosen.

questions.q: The external field threading a loop is getting WEAKER. The magnetic field produced by the induced current, inside the loop, points:
options: opposite to the external field, since an induced field always opposes the field that produces it
in the SAME direction as the external field, replacing the flux that is being lost
nowhere - a weakening field cannot drive a current, only a strengthening one can
in the same direction at first, then reverses once the external field has fallen to zero
questions.concept: Lenz's law opposes the CHANGE, not the field
questions.why: Flux is being lost, so the induced current acts to replace it and its own field inside the loop points the same way as the external field - the deck's own wording, 'if the external field gets weaker, the induced current tries to replace the missing external field'. Option (a) is the single most common Lenz error; it is correct only when the flux is increasing, that is, half the time. Option (c) confuses a decrease with an absence: d(Phi)/dt is non-zero whether the flux rises or falls. Option (d) invents a reversal - once the external field settles at zero, d(Phi)/dt = 0 and the current simply stops; Lenz's law resists a change, it does not overshoot and undo it.

questions.q: A horizontal circular loop lies on a bench. A bar magnet is held above it with its SOUTH pole pointing down at the loop, and is then LIFTED AWAY. Seen from above, the induced current in the loop flows:
options: clockwise, since the induced field must always oppose the magnet's field
anticlockwise, so that the loop's upper face becomes a north pole and attracts the departing south pole
clockwise, because a south pole always induces a clockwise current when viewed from above
not at all, since the magnet is receding and so cannot increase the flux through the loop
questions.concept: The pole form of Lenz's law: a receding pole is attracted
questions.why: Field lines enter a south pole, so just below the downward-facing S pole the field points UPWARD and the flux through the loop is upward; lifting the magnet reduces that flux, so the induced current must maintain it - its field inside the loop points up, and by the right-hand loop rule the current is anticlockwise seen from above. The loop's top face is then a north pole, which attracts the departing south pole and resists the withdrawal, exactly as Lenz requires. Option (a) is 'oppose the field' rather than 'oppose the change', and would have the loop helping the magnet leave - the perpetual-motion direction. Option (c) attaches the answer to the pole's name alone, which would make the deflection identical on approach and on withdrawal, contradicting Faraday's experiment. Option (d) confuses 'no increase' with 'no change': a decrease induces just as large an emf at the same rate.

questions.q: A magnet dropped down a long vertical copper pipe settles to a constant terminal speed v. While it descends at that speed, the rate at which heat is produced in the pipe is:
options: zero, since the magnet is no longer accelerating and so does no net work
0.5*m*v^2, the kinetic energy the magnet carries
m*g*v, the rate at which the magnet loses gravitational potential energy
not determinable from these data, since it depends on the resistivity of the copper
questions.concept: Lenz's law is energy conservation, and terminal speed closes the energy books exactly
questions.why: At terminal speed the kinetic energy is constant, so every joule of gravitational potential energy lost must appear somewhere else, and the only sink is I^2*R heating by eddy currents in the pipe wall; the rate of loss of potential energy is m*g*v. Option (a) confuses zero acceleration with zero energy transfer - the magnet is still losing height, and the magnetic force does negative work on it at exactly that rate. Option (b) quotes an energy in joules where a power in watts was asked for; the units alone condemn it. Option (d) is the most respectable wrong answer: resistivity determines WHICH terminal speed is reached, but once v is given the energy balance fixes the heating rate with no material property needed - the mark of an argument from conservation rather than mechanism.

questions.q: A magnetic flux changes with time through a region of EMPTY SPACE, with no conductor anywhere near it. In that region there is:
options: nothing, since an emf can exist only where there are charges for it to act on
a circulating ELECTRIC field, whose line integral round any closed path equals -d(Phi)/dt whether or not a wire occupies the path
a magnetic force but no electric field, magnetic effects being unable to produce electric ones
an emf that springs into existence only at the moment a conductor is introduced
questions.concept: Faraday's law in its general form, the integral of E.dl round a loop = -d(Phi)/dt, makes no mention of wires
questions.why: A changing magnetic flux creates a circulating electric field in the space around it; a conducting loop merely supplies charges for that field to push, which we then measure as an emf. It is also why a ring encircling a solenoid has an emf although B is essentially zero at the wire. Option (a) inverts cause and detector - by the same logic a gravitational field would not exist until a mass was dropped into it. Option (c) asserts exactly the independence that Faraday's law denies: a changing B produces an E, and a changing E produces a B, which is why light exists. Option (d) makes the physics wait on the experimenter's decision, and gives no account of how the field would know to appear.

questions.q: A straight metal rod is moved at right angles to a uniform magnetic field, with NO circuit connected to it. Between its ends there is:
options: nothing at all, since an emf requires a closed circuit
a steadily GROWING potential difference, since charge keeps accumulating at the ends for as long as the motion lasts
a steady potential difference B*L*v, charge having separated until the electrostatic field it sets up balances the magnetic force q*v x B
a steady CURRENT, since the free electrons are continuously pushed along the rod by the field
questions.concept: Motional emf comes from the force q*v x B on the carriers and needs no circuit
questions.why: Each free charge is carried along at v and feels a magnetic force along the rod; charge separates towards the ends until the electrostatic field it creates exactly cancels that push, giving a steady potential difference B*L*v with the v x B end positive. The rod is a source of emf - a battery of internal emf B*L*v - whether or not anything is connected. Option (a) confuses emf with current: Faraday's law contains no resistance and says nothing about closed paths. Option (b) forgets that equilibrium is reached almost instantly, which is why the potential difference is constant rather than growing without limit. Option (d) mistakes the initial transient for a steady state: with no return path a steady current is impossible.

questions.q: Two geometrically identical single-turn loops, one of copper and one of much higher-resistance nichrome, are exposed to the SAME changing flux. Compared with the copper loop, the nichrome loop has:
options: a smaller induced emf, because emf is the product of current and resistance
the same induced emf, a smaller induced current, and a smaller force opposing the change
the same induced current, since Faraday's law fixes the current directly
a larger induced emf, since a larger resistance means a larger opposition to the change
questions.concept: Faraday's law gives the emf; Ohm's law then gives the current
questions.why: The emf depends only on N and d(Phi)/dt, identical for the two loops, so both have the same emf; the larger resistance gives a smaller current by I = emf/R, hence a smaller induced moment and a smaller opposing force - which is why an aluminium ring jumps off a solenoid and a plastic one does not, and why slotting a copper pipe removes the braking. Option (a) inverts the causal chain: I*R is what the emf drives, and here it is the current that adjusts, not the emf. Option (c) would leave R with no role and predict identical braking from a good and a poor conductor. Option (d) confuses electrical resistance with mechanical opposition - more R means LESS current and therefore LESS opposition.

questions.q: State Faraday's law of induction precisely, defining every symbol and its unit. Explain why the law contains the RATE OF CHANGE of the flux rather than the flux itself, and why Faraday's own conclusion - that 'the actual existence of the magnetic flux is not sufficient to produce the induced emf; the flux must be changing' - is the sentence the whole topic turns on. Then take the four observations of the 1831 magnet-and-ammeter experiment (magnet moved in; magnet moved out; magnet held stationary inside; loop moved instead of the magnet) and say what each one separately proves.
questions.concept: The exact statement of Faraday's law, and why the rate of change - not the flux - is the cause
questions.why: Statement: the emf induced in a circuit equals minus the rate of change of the magnetic flux linking that circuit, emf = -N d(Phi)/dt, or emf = -N*d(Phi)/dt averaged as -N*(change in Phi)/(change in t). Symbols: emf is the induced emf in volts, the energy given to unit charge by a non-electrostatic agency; N is the number of turns linked, a pure number, present because the turns are in series and their emfs add; Phi = B.A = B*A*cos(theta) is the flux through one turn in webers (1 Wb = 1 T*m^2 = 1 V*s), with B in teslas, A in m^2 and theta the angle between B and the NORMAL to the surface; t is in seconds. Since 1 Wb/s = 1 V the two sides balance dimensionally. Why the rate of change: the right-hand side is d(Phi)/dt, so a circuit responds to how fast the flux threading it is changing and to nothing else - not to B, not to Phi, not to the presence or absence of motion. A coil at rest in the strongest steady field obtainable produces exactly zero volts, while a coil in a weak but rapidly changing field can produce a large one. Why Faraday's sentence is the pivot: every standard error in this topic comes from substituting a STATE where a RATE is required, and once the sentence is fixed in mind the opening question of every problem becomes 'which of B, A or theta is changing, and how fast?'. The four observations. (i) Magnet moved in, deflection: a changing flux induces a current, and does so with no battery anywhere in the circuit. (ii) Magnet moved out, deflection the OTHER way: the SIGN of d(Phi)/dt fixes the direction, which is therefore set by the change and not by the direction of B, which was the same in both cases - this alone forces something like Lenz's law. (iii) Magnet held stationary inside, NO deflection: the decisive one, since the flux is at its largest in the whole experiment and the emf is zero. Flux does not cause emf; changing flux does. (iv) Loop moved instead of the magnet, same deflection: only the relative motion enters, because only it changes the flux; Faraday's law is a statement about the circuit, not about magnets.

questions.q: Explain what the minus sign in emf = -N d(Phi)/dt is doing, and set out the sign convention that gives it meaning - how the positive normal, the sign of the flux and the positive sense of circulation are tied to one another, and what happens if the opposite normal is chosen. Then explain why Lenz's law is NOT an additional empirical rule but conservation of energy: run the argument explicitly for a magnet pushed towards a coil closed through a resistor, saying where the dissipated energy comes from and what would follow if the induced current ran the other way. Finish with the observable consequence for a bicycle dynamo.
questions.concept: The sign convention, and Lenz's law as the first law of thermodynamics applied to induction
questions.why: What the minus sign does: it is Lenz's law written into Faraday's law. It is a statement about DIRECTION - the sense in which the induced emf drives current - and never means that the emf is a negative number of volts. The convention: choose a positive normal n for the loop's surface; Phi counts as positive when B has a component along n and negative when it opposes it. The positive sense of circulation is then fixed by the RIGHT HAND - curl the fingers the positive way round the loop and the thumb must point along n. With that pairing, emf = -d(Phi)/dt is the emf driving current in the positive circulation sense, and a negative result simply means the current runs the other way round. If the opposite normal is chosen, the sign of Phi reverses AND the positive circulation sense reverses with it, so the two changes cancel and the physical direction of the current is unaltered: the convention is bookkeeping, Lenz's law is a fact that survives any bookkeeping. The energy argument: push a magnet north-pole-first towards a coil closed through a resistor. The induced current dissipates I^2*R as heat, and that energy has exactly one source - the work you do pushing the magnet against the repulsion of the induced north pole the coil presents. If the current ran the other way the coil's near face would be a SOUTH pole, the magnet would be pulled in, it would accelerate, raising d(Phi)/dt, raising the current, raising the attraction, accelerating it further: the magnet would gain unbounded kinetic energy WHILE the resistor gained unbounded heat, with nothing supplying either. That is a perpetual-motion machine of the first kind, so the induced current cannot run that way, and Lenz's law is not an extra rule bolted on to Faraday's law but conservation of energy - which is why the minus sign could have been predicted before it was measured. The dynamo: with the lamp switched off no current flows, there is no induced field and no retarding torque, so the wheel spins nearly freely; switch the lamp on and the induced magnetic moment opposes the rotation, and the rider feels the wheel become harder to turn at once. The extra pedalling effort is precisely the electrical power lighting the lamp.

questions.q: Give the general four-step procedure for finding the direction of an induced current, then apply it in full to three cases: (i) a field OUT of the page that DECREASES to zero; (ii) no field, rising to a field OUT of the page; (iii) a bar magnet whose NORTH pole is being pushed into a coil. At each step name which right-hand rule you are using and what its thumb and fingers represent. Then explain why the statement 'the induced field always opposes the applied field' is wrong, and which of your three cases demonstrates it.
questions.concept: The four-step direction algorithm, and the difference between opposing the change and opposing the field
questions.why: The procedure. (1) Establish the direction of the external B through the loop and whether the flux is rising or falling. (2) Decide the direction the induced field INSIDE the loop must take: against B if the flux is rising, along B if it is falling, none at all if the flux is constant. (3) Convert that field into a current sense with the right hand - LOOP version: point the THUMB along the required induced field inside the loop and the FINGERS curl the way the current flows. (The deck uses the equivalent STRAIGHT-WIRE version: grip one side of the loop so that the fingers, where they pass through the interior, point along the required induced field; the thumb then gives the current in that side. Both are correct; mixing them is not.) (4) Check mechanically that the resulting force or pole opposes what is being done. (i) Field out of the page, decreasing to zero: out-of-page flux is being LOST, so the induced field inside the loop must point OUT of the page to replace it; right thumb out of the page, fingers curl ANTICLOCKWISE, so the induced current is anticlockwise - exactly as the deck's figure shows. (ii) No field rising to a field out of the page: out-of-page flux is being GAINED, so the induced field must point INTO the page; right thumb into the page, fingers curl CLOCKWISE, so the induced current is clockwise - again as the deck shows. (iii) North pole pushed into a coil: the flux is rising, so the coil's near face becomes a NORTH pole and repels the magnet; seen from the magnet, the current runs anticlockwise, since that is the sense whose right-hand thumb points back out of the coil's near face towards you. The mechanical check passes - you push against a repulsion, and the work you do is the heat produced. Why 'always opposes the applied field' is wrong: case (i) demonstrates it, because there the applied field is out of the page and the induced field is ALSO out of the page. What is opposed is the CHANGE - the loss of flux - and opposing a loss means supplying more of the same, not the opposite. The wrong rule agrees with the right one only when the flux is increasing, so it fails in half of all problems, and it fails in the very first case the deck illustrates.

questions.q: Derive the motional emf B*L*v in TWO independent ways - from Faraday's law applied to the swept area, and from the magnetic force on the charge carriers - and explain why the two must agree. Say which end of the rod is at the higher potential and how you decide. Explain why the rod is a source of emf whether or not it is connected to anything, and state the emf of a rod of length L ROTATING about one end at angular speed omega, explaining the factor that distinguishes it from B*L*v. Finally give TWO distinct situations in which a moving conductor in a magnetic field has NO emf at all.
questions.concept: Motional emf from two independent routes, and why they must agree
questions.why: Route 1, Faraday from the swept area: a rod of length L slides at speed v on rails with B perpendicular to the plane of the circuit, so the enclosed area is A = L*x, Phi = B*L*x, and |emf| = d(Phi)/dt = B*L*(dx/dt) = B*L*v. Route 2, the force on the carriers: each free charge is carried along at v and feels F = q*v x B directed ALONG the rod; charge separates towards the ends until the electrostatic field E it creates exactly balances the magnetic push, q*E = q*v*B, so E = v*B and the potential difference over the length is emf = E*L = B*L*v. Why they must agree: they are two descriptions of one experiment, and if they disagreed a circuit could be built whose energy books did not balance; more deeply, the flux rule emf = -d(Phi)/dt is the single law covering both the 'conductor moves' and the 'field changes' cases, and its consistency across the two is what makes it a law rather than a recipe. Which end is positive: the v x B end. Evaluate the cross product for the actual geometry rather than guessing; conventional positive charge is pushed towards that end, so it is the + terminal and the electrons pile up at the other. Why the rod is a source with or without a circuit: an emf is energy per unit charge supplied by a NON-ELECTROSTATIC agency, here the magnetic force, and it exists in the rod whether or not charge has anywhere to go. Disconnected, the rod is a battery on open circuit - full emf B*L*v, zero current; close the circuit through R and the same emf drives I = B*L*v/R, which feels F = B*I*L = B^2*L^2*v/R against the motion, the retarding force that makes the mechanical power F*v equal the electrical power I^2*R exactly. Rotating rod: a rod pivoted at one end and turning at omega in a field B parallel to the rotation axis has emf = 0.5*B*L^2*omega. The factor 0.5 appears because the speed is NOT uniform along the rod - zero at the pivot, L*omega at the tip - so integrating the element contributions B*(omega*r)*dr from 0 to L gives 0.5*B*L^2*omega, equivalently B*L*v_mean with v_mean = 0.5*L*omega. Using the tip speed gives exactly twice the correct answer. Two cases with no emf: (i) the rod moves ALONG its own length, so it sweeps no area and v x B is perpendicular to the rod, driving no charge from end to end; (ii) the rod moves PARALLEL to B, so v x B = 0 and no flux is swept. (A third worth knowing: a closed loop translating entirely INSIDE a large uniform field, where B, A and theta are all constant, so d(Phi)/dt = 0 despite the motion.)

checks.topic: Decomposition and modularisation as concepts: the definition of modularisation and the coupling and cohesion conditions carried by its two clauses, why the course says we decompose at all, the five stated advantages and the five stated disadvantages, the single responsibility principle, cohesion and coupling with how each is judged and which direction each should go, information hiding and its three benefits, refactoring and its defining test, horizontal versus vertical structural partitioning, software architecture and its three constituents, the three levels of software pattern, and top-down versus bottom-up design

questions.q: The course defines modularisation as dividing a program's functionality into independent modules such that each independent module has everything it needs to implement only a part of the program's functionality. The definition carries two separate conditions. Which design fault does each one rule out?
options: Both conditions rule out the same fault stated twice - a module that is too large - the first by size and the second by scope

'Everything it needs' rules out a module that cannot work until other modules assist it, which is coupling; 'only a part' rules out a module that has taken on more than one part of the functionality, which is cohesion
'Everything it needs' rules out duplicated code, since a module that has everything need never copy from elsewhere; 'only a part' rules out a module being reused in a second program
'Everything it needs' requires every module to hold its own copy of the program's data; 'only a part' requires that no module be visible to any other
questions.concept: The definition of modularisation states the coupling condition and the cohesion condition in one sentence
questions.why: 'Each independent module has everything it needs' is the demand for independence - a module that must first ask another module for help does not have everything it needs, and that is exactly coupling, the extent to which modules depend on other modules before performing their function. 'To implement only a part of the program's functionality' is the demand for one job - a module implementing two parts is the module the single responsibility principle forbids, and it is exactly low cohesion. Option a reads both halves as being about size; neither mentions size, and a large module can satisfy both while a tiny one can fail both. Option c borrows Week 8's 'prevents the duplication of codes', which is a benefit of writing a function once, not a clause of this definition, and its second half inverts a stated advantage, since the course says modules can easily be used in another program. Option d makes two impossible demands: duplicating the program's data in every module would guarantee inconsistency, and modules invisible to one another could never be assembled into a program.

questions.q: The course opens with a function of more than five thousand lines and asks how stressful it would be to change part of it. What, precisely, is the fault being complained of?
options: That the function is too long to read in one sitting, so no single developer can hold it in mind well enough to work on it
That a function of that size will exceed the compiler's limits and must be broken up before it will build at all

That changing a part of the code can affect other parts of the code, so no change can be made in isolation - which is why the stated cure is being able to change different parts without affecting other parts
That a five-thousand-line function must contain duplicated code somewhere, and duplication is the fault that decomposition exists to remove
questions.concept: The stated problem is change propagation, not length
questions.why: The deck's sentence is 'changing a part of the code can even affect other parts of the code', and the cure it states is the exact negation: modularisation ensures that we are able to make changes to different parts of our code without affecting other parts of the code. Length is only how the entanglement is noticed. Option a is the plausible half-truth that costs the mark: readability is a listed advantage of modularisation (understanding a small module and function is easier), but it is not the fault this slide is about, and a five-thousand-line function that touched nothing else would still be readable one screen at a time. Option b invents a compiler limit; nothing in the deck concerns compiler capacity, and the deck in fact lists longer compilation time as a disadvantage of modularising. Option d assumes duplication must be present; a long function may contain none and still be impossible to change safely, which is why the deck's complaint is stated in terms of effects, not repetition.

questions.q: A team modularises a working program. Afterwards the build takes noticeably longer, the compiled program is larger, and it runs slightly slower. What should they conclude?
options: That these are three of the course's five stated disadvantages of modularisation itself - the price paid for the advantages, incurred by the module boundaries that control and data must now cross
That they have produced low cohesion, since a slower and larger program is the standard symptom of functions that do not serve one aim
That they have produced high coupling, since a longer build means the modules are being recompiled because of one another
That they have modularised something that should not have been modularised, since a correct modularisation leaves execution time, size and build time unchanged
questions.concept: The five disadvantages are the cost of modularisation as such
questions.why: The course lists them: execution time may be longer, storage size may be increased, compilation and loading time may be longer, inter-module communication problems may be increased, and it demands more initial design time. Each is caused mechanically by having boundaries at all - a boundary is a place control and data must cross, and separately stored, separately compiled units are separately loaded. Options b and c are the vocabulary answers: they reach for the two words everyone remembers and attach them to symptoms that are not diagnostic of either. Low cohesion shows itself as a module that cannot be described in one phrase; high coupling shows itself as a change in one module forcing changes in another. Neither is measured on a stopwatch. Option d states the opposite of the deck - if modularisation were free of cost there would be no disadvantages slide, and no reason to warn that it demands more initial design time.

questions.q: Cohesion is judged by which question?
options: How many other modules this module has to call before it can complete its work
How frequently the functions inside the module call one another, since a module whose functions never call each other has not been joined together at all
How small the module is, since the course's advantages are all stated of smaller modules and functions

Whether the functions in the module work together to achieve the ultimate aim of the module - so functions that never call one another are cohesive if they serve that one aim, and functions that call each other constantly are not if they are collectively serving several
questions.concept: Cohesion is judged against the module's single ultimate aim
questions.why: The definition is that cohesion describes the extent to which the functions in a module work together to achieve the ultimate aim of the module. The test therefore names an aim and asks whether every function serves it. Option a is the definition of coupling, asked outward rather than inward - the commonest confusion in the topic, and the reason so many scripts answer both questions with the same sentence. Option b is the trap this question exists for: mutual calling is neither necessary nor sufficient. A validate function and a send_confirmation function never call each other and both serve one aim; the deck's own refactoring example is a component whose four functions have a limited relationship with one another - the fault is four aims, not silence between them. Option c confuses cohesion with size; the advantages of smallness are listed separately, and a small module holding two unrelated functions has low cohesion precisely because it is not small enough to have one aim.

questions.q: Module 'report' contains a single line that reads records[cid][7] from module 'customer', and nothing else. Module 'invoice' calls three published functions of 'customer' two hundred times. On the course's definition, which is more tightly coupled to 'customer'?
options: 'invoice', because coupling describes the extent to which modules depend on one another and two hundred calls is a far greater extent of dependence than one

'report', because coupling is the extent to which a module depends on another before it can perform its function, and 'report' depends on 'customer''s internal data structure and field order, which changes whenever 'customer' is reorganised
They are equally coupled, since both reach outside themselves and coupling records only whether a dependency exists, not what it is on
Neither is coupled at all, because coupling is a property measured between whole subsystems, whereas both of these are single modules within one subsystem
questions.concept: Coupling counts what a module must depend on, not how often it speaks
questions.why: Coupling is the extent to which modules depend on other modules before performing their function. 'report' cannot perform its function unless 'customer' stores records in a structure indexed by cid with the discount in field 7 - so it depends on 'customer''s data structures, which is exactly what information hiding says must not be accessible. Reorder the fields, or move the records into a database, and 'report' breaks silently while still compiling. 'invoice' depends only on three published functions continuing to answer the same questions; two hundred calls change nothing about what it must know. Option a is the 'coupling means traffic' belief, which counts the wrong thing entirely and would make every well-designed system look tightly coupled. Option c reduces coupling to a yes/no, but the word is extent - it is precisely a matter of degree, and the degree is set by what is depended upon. Option d invents a rule that coupling applies only between subsystems; the deck states it of modules in a project.

questions.q: Which statement about information hiding is correct?
options: Modules should pass as little information to one another as they possibly can, and a module that receives less than it needs is preferable to one that receives more
Information hiding means the source code of a module is kept from other teams, which is why the course lists it among the security measures of a design
The data structures and processing details of one module are not accessible to other modules, and modules pass only that much information as is required to accomplish the software functions
Information hiding is the practice of storing each module in its own file so that a developer working on one module cannot see the contents of another
questions.concept: What information hiding hides, and the force of the word 'required'
questions.why: The deck: the data structures and processing details of one module are not accessible to other modules, and they pass only that much information to each other, which is required to accomplish the software functions. Option a is the most instructive wrong answer, because it is the same sentence with 'required' deleted. Passing less than is required does not hide anything; it produces a module that cannot do its job, and the deck's phrasing sets the floor at what the functions need. Option b is the Week 8 error at module scale: hiding is about what other code may reach and depend upon, not about who may read the source - perfectly public source can still hide its data structures behind an interface. Option d confuses a file with an interface. Putting modules in separate files is something modularisation permits; it hides nothing if the second module can still read the first one's structures.

questions.q: Designer A splits a module that had been doing four loosely-related jobs into four modules; for every input the system's outputs are identical to before. Designer B changes a module so that it now also emails a receipt. Which has refactored, and what is the test?
options: Both have: each has improved the design, and refactoring is any change made to improve the internal quality of a system
A only: refactoring modifies a software system to improve the internal structure of design without changing its external behaviour, and B's change is externally visible
B only: A has merely moved code between files, and refactoring requires that the design be genuinely improved, which splitting alone does not achieve
Neither: refactoring means reducing the complexity of module design, and A increased the number of modules while B added work
questions.concept: Refactoring is defined by unchanged external behaviour
questions.why: Refactoring can be defined as a process of modifying a software system to improve the internal structure of design without changing its external behaviour, and it reduces the complexity of module design while keeping its behaviour or function unchanged. A's split leaves every output identical, which is exactly the deck's own worked example: a component with low cohesion performing four functions of limited relationship is refactored into four components each with high cohesion, leading to easier integration, testing and maintenance. B's receipt email is a new externally observable act, so whatever its merits it is not a refactoring. Option a drops the defining clause and calls any improvement a refactoring - which destroys the point of the word, since refactoring's whole value is the promise that if behaviour changed, something went wrong. Option c demands a different test of improvement; the deck's improvement is precisely the move from low to high cohesion, which is what A did. Option d misreads 'reduces the complexity of module design' as 'reduces the number of modules'; the deck's example increases the count from one to four and calls that a reduction in complexity.

questions.q: Which single feature separates an idiom from an architectural pattern and a design pattern?
options: It is the only one of the three that is intended to be reused, the other two being descriptions of a particular system rather than solutions to recurring problems
It is the only one concerned with the interaction between software components, the other two being concerned only with structure
It is the smallest, being a pattern that occupies fewer lines than a design pattern, which in turn occupies fewer than an architectural pattern

It is programming-language specific - it describes the implementation of a component, and the method of interaction among components, in a specific programming language, which is why idioms are also called coding patterns
questions.concept: The level and the language-dependence of the three pattern types
questions.why: Idioms are low-level patterns which are programming-language specific; they describe the implementation of a software component, the method used for interaction among software components, etc., in a specific programming language, and are often termed coding patterns. That is the only property that separates them cleanly. Option a inverts the definition of a pattern altogether: a pattern is by definition a description of the solution to a recurring design problem in such a way that the solution can be used again and again, so reusability is common to all three.
