Option b is a real trap, because design patterns explicitly address mechanisms that affect component-to-component interaction; interaction is therefore not the discriminator, and an answer that reaches for it has read only the idiom slide. Option c invents a size ordering. High, medium and low describe the level of strategy - architecture, refinement of elements, implementation - not the number of lines.

questions.q: Define cohesion and coupling in the course's words. For each, say where the measurement is taken and which direction it should go. Then explain why a team that removes a dependency by merging two modules into one has not improved the design, even though the coupling between those two modules is now zero. Finish with the car analogy: what do the steering wheel, radiator, battery and brake show about cohesion, and what does the starter's dependence on the battery show about coupling?
questions.concept: Cohesion and coupling - two readings, two places, opposite directions, and why merging is a counterfeit fix
questions.why: Cohesion describes the extent to which the functions in a module work together to achieve the ultimate aim of the module, and we usually want high cohesion. Coupling describes the extent to which modules depend on other modules before performing their function, and since we want our modules to be independent we usually want low coupling. Cohesion is a reading taken inside a single module: name the module's one aim, then ask of each function whether it serves that aim. Coupling is a reading taken between modules: name the boundary, then ask what one module must know about the other before it can work. Because they are taken in different places they are not two ends of one scale, and a design can be bad on both at once. On merging: suppose 'orders' calls 'stock' and a team merges them into 'sales'. The coupling between 'orders' and 'stock' is now zero, but only because there is no longer an 'orders' and a 'stock' to measure between. The dependency itself has not been removed - the same code still needs the same information at the same moment. What has changed is that it now runs inside a module, where no interface governs it and nobody can see it; the boundary that made the dependency explicit, reviewable and narrow has been deleted rather than tightened. Cohesion has fallen at the same time, because 'sales' now has two responsibilities and so breaks the single responsibility principle, which demands that modules should not have more than a single responsibility. The genuine fix is the opposite operation: keep the boundary and narrow the interface, so that 'orders' depends on one published question rather than on 'stock''s internals. The test to apply is not 'did a number improve' but 'if stock is reorganised internally, must orders change?'. The car analogy: the car transports passengers, and the steering wheel, radiator, battery and brake each exist for one aim - steering, cooling, storing charge, stopping - so each is highly cohesive, which is why a fault can be diagnosed to a part and a part replaced on its own. The starter, however, plainly depends on the battery, so the parts are not unconnected, and this is the point students miss. What makes the coupling low is that the starter needs only twelve volts at two terminals: it does not know the battery's chemistry, its plate arrangement or its internal wiring, so a different battery of the same terminals works and no part of the starter changes. Low coupling is a real dependency running through a narrow, defined interface, not the absence of dependency; a part that depended on nothing would do nothing.

questions.q: State the course's definition of information hiding and its three stated benefits. Say precisely what is hidden, from whom, and what still crosses the boundary. Then explain why information hiding is the mechanism that produces low coupling rather than a separate good habit - and name the one thing information hiding is commonly, and wrongly, taken to mean.
questions.concept: Information hiding - what is hidden, from whom, and why it is the cause of low coupling
questions.why: The definition: modules should be specified and designed in such a way that the data structures and processing details of one module are not accessible to other modules. They pass only that much information to each other, which is required to accomplish the software functions. The way of hiding unnecessary details is referred to as information hiding. The three benefits: it emphasises communication through controlled interfaces; it decreases the probability of adverse effects; it restricts the effects of changes in one component on others. What is hidden is the data structures - how the module stores what it stores - and the processing details - how it does what it does. From whom: from other modules, that is, from other code. What still crosses the boundary is the module's service, and exactly as much information as the software functions require; the word 'required' sets a floor, so information hiding is never an argument for starving a caller of what it needs. Why it is the mechanism rather than a habit: coupling is the extent to which modules depend on other modules before performing their function, and a module can only depend on what it can reach. If the data structures and processing details are inaccessible then no other module can be written to depend on them, however careless its author; the only thing left to depend on is the published interface, which is why the first stated benefit is that communication is forced through controlled interfaces. The third benefit then follows automatically - if nothing outside depended on the internals, changing the internals restricts the effects of changes in one component on others to nothing at all. So low coupling is not achieved by exhortation but by inaccessibility: information hiding removes the possibility of the dependency, and low coupling is the reading you take afterwards. It is the same bargain as Week 8's functional abstraction - a caller gets a name and the input and output formats - stated one scale up, at the module rather than the function. The common misreading is that information hiding means keeping source code secret from people. It does not: the target is other modules, and a module whose source is published in full still hides information if nothing outside it can reach its structures. The second, subtler misreading is treating 'pass only that much information' as 'pass as little as possible'; the sentence ends 'which is required to accomplish the software functions'.

questions.q: Give the course's definition of software architecture, naming all three things the structure contains, and the three reasons the course gives for needing it. Then set out the three levels of software pattern, saying for each what level of strategy it is, what it addresses, and what the course says it is often considered equivalent to.
questions.concept: Software architecture and the three levels of software pattern
questions.why: Software architecture refers to the structure of the system, which contains various components of a program or system, the attributes (properties) of those components, and the relationship between them. All three parts are examinable, and an answer naming only the components has given a third of the definition. The course adds that the software architecture enables the software engineers to analyze the software design efficiently. The three stated reasons: it enables efficient communication between all the interested stakeholders; it highlights early design decisions that affect activities such as coding and testing; and it creates intellectual models of how the system is organized into components and how these components interact with each other. All three are about people and foresight - an architecture is a thing to talk about and decide with, before there is code to inspect. A software pattern provides a description of the solution to a recurring design problem of some specific domain in such a way that the solution can be used again and again; its objective is to give a designer insight enough to determine whether the pattern can be reused, whether it is applicable to the current project, and whether it can be used to develop a similar but functionally or structurally different design pattern. The three levels: architectural patterns are high-level strategies referring to the overall structure and organization of a software system, defining its elements such as subsystems, components and classes, and indicating the relationship between the elements along with the rules and guidelines for specifying these relationships - often considered equivalent to software architecture. Design patterns are medium-level strategies used to solve design problems, providing a means for the refinement of the elements defined by an architectural pattern or the relationship among them, and addressing specific design elements such as the relationship among components or mechanisms that affect component-to-component interaction - often considered equivalent to software components. Idioms are low-level patterns which are programming-language specific, describing the implementation of a software component and the method used for interaction among software components in a specific programming language - often termed coding patterns. The ordering is one of decreasing scope and increasing commitment: architecture says what the parts are, design says how a part is refined and how parts interact, and the idiom says how that is written in C or Python.

questions.q: Contrast top-down and bottom-up design: where each starts, what operation each performs, what happens to the amount of abstraction, and the circumstance in which the course says each is the more suitable. Then explain the course's claim that the two approaches are not individually practicable - what specifically goes wrong if a project uses only one of them?
questions.concept: The two design approaches, and why each alone runs out of information
questions.why: Top-down design starts by taking the whole software system as one entity and decomposes it to achieve more than one sub-system or component based on some characteristics. Each sub-system is then treated as a system in its own right and decomposed further, and the process keeps running until the lowest level of system in the top-down hierarchy is achieved. It starts with a generalized model of the system and keeps on defining the more specific part of it, and when all components are composed the whole system comes into existence. It is more suitable when the software solution needs to be designed from scratch and specific details are unknown - precisely the situation in which you can describe the whole but not yet the parts. Bottom-up design starts with the most specific and basic components, proceeds with composing higher level components by using basic or lower level components, and keeps creating higher level components until the desired system is evolved as one single component; with each higher level, the amount of abstraction is increased. It is more suitable when a system needs to be created from some existing system, where the basic primitives can be used in the newer system - that is, when the parts already exist and the question is what to build out of them. The course states flatly that top-down and bottom-up approaches are not individually practicable and that a good combination of both is used. The reason is that each runs out of information at the end furthest from where it started. Pure top-down keeps subdividing on the assumption that whatever a sub-problem needs will exist when it gets there; at the bottom it meets the primitives that actually exist - the libraries, the database, the modules already written - and if these do not match the shape the decomposition assumed, the split has to be redone, and the deeper the hierarchy the more of it is wasted. Pure bottom-up has the opposite failure: it composes excellent, highly cohesive components upward without any statement of the system's ultimate aim, so it can produce a fine set of parts that assemble into the wrong system, or into one whose top-level structure nobody can describe to a stakeholder - which is exactly what the architecture slide says an architecture is for. In practice the top-down decomposition supplies the aims and the boundaries, the bottom-up composition supplies the primitives and the reality check, and the design converges from both ends; whichever direction you travel in, the cut you make is judged by cohesion, coupling and information hiding.

checks.topic: Volume problems carried out: finding the intersections that give the limits, writing outer and inner radii as distances from the axis, squaring before integrating, setting up shells with radius times height times thickness, rotating about the lines y = k and x = h, and checking one method against the other - with the squaring, radius, limit and dx-versus-dy traps at every step.

questions.q: The region under y = x + 1 from x = 0 to x = 2, revolved about the x-axis, has volume:
options: 4*pi
9*pi
questions.concept: Disc method: square the radius first, then integrate, then subtract at both limits.
questions.why: R(x) = x + 1, so V = pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of (x + 1)^2 dx) = pi*[(x + 1)^3/3] from 0 to 2 = pi*(27/3 - 1/3) = 26*pi/3. (b) is pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of (x + 1) dx) = 4*pi - the radius was never squared, so an area has been reported as a volume. (c) is pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of x^2 dx) = 8*pi/3, obtained by squaring only the x and dropping the +1, i.e. rotating y = x instead. (d) is pi*[(x + 1)^3/3] evaluated at the upper limit alone, 27*pi/3 = 9*pi; the lower limit contributes (0 + 1)^3/3 = 1/3 and is not zero just because x = 0.

questions.q: The region enclosed by y = x^2 and y = 4, revolved about the x-axis, has volume:
questions.concept: Washer: the outer radius is the boundary further from the axis, and the squares are taken before the subtraction.
questions.why: Intersections: x^2 = 4 -> x = -2 and x = 2. The axis is y = 0, and on (-2, 2) the line y = 4 is further from it than the parabola, so R = 4 and r = x^2. V = pi*(integral from -2 to 2 of (16 - x^4) dx) = pi*[16x - x^5/5] from -2 to 2 = pi*(64 - 64/5) = 256*pi/5. (a) is pi*(integral from -2 to 2 of (4 - x^2) dx) = 32*pi/3, the Week 10 AREA multiplied by pi, with no squaring anywhere. (b) is the integral taken from 0 to 2 only, exactly half, the classic loss of the symmetric left-hand half. (d) is pi*(integral from -2 to 2 of (4 - x^2)^2 dx) = 512*pi/15, the (R - r)^2 error - and note it is smaller than the true answer, as (R - r)^2 < R^2 - r^2 always is when r > 0.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = sqrt(x), y = 0 and x = 4, revolved about the y-axis, has volume:
options: 8*pi
questions.concept: Shells about a vertical axis: radius x, height y, thickness dx, and the factor is 2*pi.
questions.why: V = 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 4 of x*sqrt(x) dx) = 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 4 of x^(3/2) dx) = 2*pi*[(2/5)*x^(5/2)] from 0 to 4 = 2*pi*(2/5)*32 = 128*pi/5. (c) is 64*pi/5, the same integral with pi instead of 2*pi - the shell factor is a circumference, not an area. (b) is 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 4 of sqrt(x) dx) = 32*pi/3, in which the radius x was omitted and only the height integrated, so every shell has been given radius 1. (a) is 8*pi, the volume of the SAME region about the x-axis by discs - the right region, the wrong axis, and a warning that a plausible-looking number proves nothing about the set-up.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = x^2, y = 0, x = 0 and x = 1, revolved about the line y = 2, has volume:
options: pi/5
questions.concept: The radius is the distance from the axis, and an axis lying above the region makes the LOWEST boundary the outer one.
questions.why: The region runs from y = 0 up to y = x^2 on [0, 1], and every point of it is below y = 2. The furthest boundary from the axis is y = 0, giving R = 2 - 0 = 2; the nearest is the parabola, giving r = 2 - x^2. V = pi*(integral from 0 to 1 of (4 - (2 - x^2)^2) dx) = pi*(integral from 0 to 1 of (4x^2 - x^4) dx) = pi*(4/3 - 1/5) = 17*pi/15. (d) is 23*pi/15, from using R = x^2 + 2 - the shift was added instead of subtracted, which is correct for an axis BELOW the region and wrong for one above it. (b) is pi*(integral from 0 to 1 of x^4 dx) = pi/5, the volume about y = 0, i.e. the shift ignored entirely. (a) is the correct integrand with R and r interchanged, and a negative volume is always the signature of that swap, never something to repair with a modulus.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = x^3, y = 0 and x = 2 is revolved about the line x = 2. The correct set-up is:
options: 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of (x - 2)*x^3 dx)
2*pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of (2 - x)*x^3 dx)
2*pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of x*x^3 dx)
pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of (2 - x)^2 dx)
questions.concept: A shell's radius is the distance from the axis, so for a region lying to the left of x = 2 it is 2 - x.
questions.why: The axis is vertical, so shells are vertical and the variable is dx; the shell at x has radius 2 - x (non-negative on [0, 2]), height x^3 - 0, thickness dx, giving 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of (2 - x)*x^3 dx). (a) reverses the radius to x - 2, which is negative throughout the interval and delivers the true volume with a minus sign. (c) uses radius x, which is the distance from the Y-AXIS - it silently answers a different question, and it is the error that survives longest because the integral is perfectly easy. (d) applies the disc formula pi*(integral of R^2 dx) to a shell radius; the disc formula needs slices perpendicular to the axis, and slices perpendicular to a vertical axis are stacked in y, so a dx there is impossible on its own terms.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = x^2, the y-axis and the line y = 4 (first quadrant), revolved about the y-axis, has volume:
options: 8*pi
questions.concept: Discs about a vertical axis are stacked in y, so the curve must be inverted and the limits must be y-values.
questions.why: x = sqrt(y), R(y) = sqrt(y), and y runs from 0 to 4: V = pi*(integral from 0 to 4 of (sqrt(y))^2 dy) = pi*(integral from 0 to 4 of y dy) = 8*pi. (c) is pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of x^4 dx) = 32*pi/5, the disc formula applied in x, which computes the solid formed by rotating the region under the parabola about the X-axis - a different region and a different axis. (d) is pi*(integral from 0 to 4 of y^2 dy) = 64*pi/3, obtained by renaming x as y in 'pi*(integral of x^2)' without ever inverting the relation - the commonest of all dy errors, because it looks like a change of variable and is only a change of letter. (b) is 16*pi/3, which is pi times the Week 10 area of this region, the reflex of decorating an area with pi.

questions.q: The region under y = sqrt(9 - x^2), -3 <= x <= 3, revolved about the x-axis, has volume:
options: 18*pi
36*pi
72*pi
questions.concept: Revolving a semicircular region of radius r about its diameter generates the sphere, V = 4*pi*r^3/3.
questions.why: R(x) = sqrt(9 - x^2), so R^2 = 9 - x^2 and V = pi*(integral from -3 to 3 of (9 - x^2) dx) = pi*[9x - x^3/3] from -3 to 3 = pi*(18 + 18) = 36*pi, which is 4*pi*3^3/3. (a) is 18*pi, the integral from 0 to 3 only - half the interval, and the fact that it is exactly half the right answer makes it very easy to accept. (c) is pi*(integral from -3 to 3 of sqrt(9 - x^2) dx) = pi*(9*pi/2) = 9*pi^2/2, the radius never squared; a pi^2 in a volume is always a sign that an area formula has been used where a squared radius belonged. (d) is 72*pi, from doubling 36*pi on the grounds that the semicircle has 'two halves' about the axis - but the upper and lower halves sweep the SAME ball, and counting both counts the sphere twice.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = x^2, y = 0, x = 1 and x = 2, revolved about the y-axis, has volume:
questions.concept: Shells with an inner limit: the radius is still x, and the limits are the x-values that bound the region.
questions.why: V = 2*pi*(integral from 1 to 2 of x*x^2 dx) = 2*pi*[x^4/4] from 1 to 2 = 2*pi*(4 - 1/4) = 15*pi/2. (a) is 15*pi/4, the same integral with pi in place of 2*pi. (b) is 2*pi*(integral from 1 to 2 of (x - 1)*x^2 dx) = 17*pi/6, from taking the radius as x - 1 because the region starts at x = 1 - but the radius is the distance from the AXIS OF REVOLUTION, not from the near edge of the region, and the axis is x = 0. (d) is pi*(integral from 1 to 2 of x^4 dx) = 31*pi/5, the disc formula in x, which cannot describe a rotation about a vertical axis at all. Note that this solid is a genuine tube with a cylindrical hole of radius 1, and any correct method must reflect that.

questions.q: The region enclosed by y = 2x and y = x^2 is revolved (i) about the x-axis and (ii) about the y-axis. Find both volumes, showing how you obtain the limits, which boundary is outer in each case and why, and which method you use for each and why.
questions.concept: The same region gives two different solids about two different axes, and which boundary is 'outer' is decided by distance from the axis, not by which curve is higher on the page.
questions.why: Limits first: 2x = x^2 -> x*(x - 2) = 0 -> x = 0 and x = 2, so the region runs from (0, 0) to (2, 4). Test x = 1: the line gives y = 2, the parabola y = 1, so the LINE is above the parabola throughout. (i) ABOUT THE x-AXIS. Slices perpendicular to a horizontal axis are stacked in x, so this is a washer integral in dx. The distance from y = 0 to the line is 2x and to the parabola is x^2; the line is above and both are positive, so R = 2x and r = x^2. V = pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of ((2x)^2 - (x^2)^2) dx) = pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of (4x^2 - x^4) dx) = pi*[4x^3/3 - x^5/5] from 0 to 2 = pi*(32/3 - 32/5) = 64*pi/15. (ii) ABOUT THE y-AXIS. Both boundaries are given as y = f(x), so shells avoid inverting anything: the shell at x has radius x, height (top minus bottom) = 2x - x^2, thickness dx, and x still runs 0 to 2. V = 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of x*(2x - x^2) dx) = 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of (2x^2 - x^3) dx) = 2*pi*[2x^3/3 - x^4/4] from 0 to 2 = 2*pi*(16/3 - 4) = 8*pi/3. The two numbers differ because they are different solids: about the x-axis the far boundary is the line, while about the y-axis the far boundary from the axis is the PARABOLA (at height y, x = sqrt(y) lies further out than x = y/2), so the 'top' curve of part (i) has become the inner boundary in part (ii). Nothing about the picture in x tells you which is outer; only distance from the stated axis does.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = x^3, y = 0 and x = 2 is revolved about the y-axis. Evaluate the volume twice - once by shells and once by washers - showing the limits, the radii and the inversion in full, and say what the agreement of the two numbers does and does not prove about your working.
questions.concept: Shells and washers slice the same solid in perpendicular directions, so they must agree; their agreement checks the arithmetic and the radii, but not the region.
questions.why: BY SHELLS (axis vertical -> vertical tubes -> dx). Radius x, height x^3 - 0, limits x = 0 to 2: V = 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of x*x^3 dx) = 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of x^4 dx) = 2*pi*[x^5/5] from 0 to 2 = 2*pi*(32/5) = 64*pi/5. BY WASHERS (axis vertical -> horizontal annuli -> dy). Invert the curve: y = x^3 -> x = y^(1/3). The solid's corner is (2, 8), so y runs 0 to 8. At height y the solid runs from the curve out to the line x = 2, so the inner radius is y^(1/3) and the outer radius is the constant 2: V = pi*(integral from 0 to 8 of (2^2 - (y^(1/3))^2) dy) = pi*(integral from 0 to 8 of (4 - y^(2/3)) dy) = pi*[4y - (3/5)*y^(5/3)] from 0 to 8 = pi*(32 - (3/5)*32) = 32*pi*(1 - 3/5) = 64*pi/5, using 8^(5/3) = 2^5 = 32. WHAT THE AGREEMENT PROVES: that the squaring, the inversion, the limits and the integration are consistent - two independent routes with different integrands, different variables and different limits landing on the same number is very strong evidence that none of those steps is wrong. WHAT IT DOES NOT PROVE: that you revolved the right region about the right axis. Both calculations started from the same reading of the question, so a misread boundary (taking x = 2 as y = 2, say) would corrupt both identically and they would still agree. The check is on the machinery, not on the interpretation - for that you need the sketch.

questions.q: The region bounded by y = sqrt(x), y = 0 and x = 4 is revolved about the line y = 2. Set up and evaluate the volume, stating the outer and inner radii as distances. Then say what number you would have obtained had you written the inner radius as sqrt(x) - 2, and what solid, if any, that corresponds to.
questions.concept: Rotating about y = 2 makes every radius a distance from that line, and the boundary furthest from the line is the outer one - here the x-axis, not the curve.
questions.why: On [0, 4] the region lies between y = 0 and y = sqrt(x), and sqrt(4) = 2, so the curve just reaches the axis of revolution at the right-hand end and the region lies entirely BELOW y = 2. Distances from the axis: to y = 0 it is 2 - 0 = 2 (outer); to the curve it is 2 - sqrt(x) (inner), running from 2 down to 0. V = pi*(integral from 0 to 4 of (2^2 - (2 - sqrt(x))^2) dx) = pi*(integral from 0 to 4 of (4 - (4 - 4*sqrt(x) + x)) dx) = pi*(integral from 0 to 4 of (4*sqrt(x) - x) dx) = pi*[(8/3)*x^(3/2) - x^2/2] from 0 to 4 = pi*(64/3 - 8) = 40*pi/3. (Check by shells, which about a horizontal axis run in dy: radius 2 - y, height 4 - y^2, y from 0 to 2, giving 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of (2 - y)*(4 - y^2) dy) = 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 2 of (8 - 4y - 2y^2 + y^3) dy) = 2*pi*(16 - 8 - 16/3 + 4) = 2*pi*(20/3) = 40*pi/3.) Had the inner radius been written as sqrt(x) - 2, it would have been negative everywhere on [0, 4), but squaring hides that: (sqrt(x) - 2)^2 = (2 - sqrt(x))^2, so this particular slip happens to give the same 40*pi/3. That is exactly why it is dangerous - the sign error is invisible here and fatal elsewhere, for instance the moment the region straddles the line and the two expressions stop describing the same distance. The error that does change the answer is using sqrt(x) + 2 or plain sqrt(x) as a radius: sqrt(x) alone gives pi*(integral from 0 to 4 of x dx) = 8*pi, the volume about y = 0, i.e. the shift forgotten. Radii must be checked for non-negativity BEFORE they are squared, not after.

questions.q: The region enclosed by y = x - x^2 and the x-axis is revolved about the y-axis. Explain why the washer method is impractical here and the shell method is not, set up the shell integral with its radius, height and limits justified, and evaluate it.
questions.concept: Shells need the boundary as y = f(x) and washers need it as x = g(y), so a curve that cannot be inverted single-valuedly decides the method for you.
questions.why: The region: y = x - x^2 meets y = 0 where x*(1 - x) = 0, i.e. x = 0 and x = 1, and the parabola opens downward, so the region is the arch above the x-axis on [0, 1] with maximum y = 1/4 at x = 1/2. WHY WASHERS ARE IMPRACTICAL: about the y-axis, washers are horizontal annuli at height y and they need the TWO x-values on the curve at that height - the roots of x^2 - x + y = 0, namely x = (1 +- sqrt(1 - 4y))/2. The parabola is not one-to-one on [0, 1], so the inversion produces two branches: the left branch is the inner radius and the right branch is the outer, y runs only from 0 to 1/4, and the integrand becomes pi*[((1 + sqrt(1 - 4y))/2)^2 - ((1 - sqrt(1 - 4y))/2)^2] = pi*sqrt(1 - 4y). It is doable here, but it required solving a quadratic and identifying which root is which - and for a cubic such as y = 2x^2 - x^3 the same step is impossible. SHELLS: the axis is vertical, so the tubes are vertical and the variable is dx, with no inversion at all. The tube at x has radius x (its distance from the y-axis), height (top minus bottom) = (x - x^2) - 0, thickness dx, and x runs over the region, 0 to 1: V = 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 1 of x*(x - x^2) dx) = 2*pi*(integral from 0 to 1 of (x^2 - x^3) dx) = 2*pi*[x^3/3 - x^4/4] from 0 to 1 = 2*pi*(1/3 - 1/4) = 2*pi/12 = pi/6. (The washer route confirms it: pi*(integral from 0 to 1/4 of sqrt(1 - 4y) dy) = pi*[-(1/6)*(1 - 4y)^(3/2)] from 0 to 1/4 = pi/6 - the same solid, far more work, and two chances to attach the branches the wrong way round.)

checks.topic: Numerical Faraday and Lenz work: computing Phi = B*A*cos(theta) with the angle taken from the normal and areas converted to m^2, emf from N*A*(dB/dt) and from N*(change in Phi)/(change in t), the factor of two when a coil is flipped through 180 degrees rather than turned through 90 degrees, induced charge q = N*(change in Phi)/R and its independence of the time taken, motional emf B*L*v with the retarding force B^2*L^2*v/R and a closed power audit, the rotating rod 0.5*B*L^2*omega with the 2*pi*f and tip-speed traps, geometries in which the emf is exactly zero, and the solenoid-and-ring case in which the flux is that of the enclosed area and not of the coil.

questions.q: A flat square coil of 40 turns and side 0.15 m is placed in a uniform field of 0.60 T with the PLANE of the coil making an angle of 30 degrees with the field. The flux through ONE turn is:
questions.concept: Phi = B*A*cos(theta) with theta measured from the NORMAL, not from the plane
questions.why: A = (0.15)^2 = 2.25 x 10^-2 m^2. The PLANE is at 30 degrees to B, so the NORMAL is at 60 degrees: Phi = B*A*cos(60 degrees) = (0.60)(2.25 x 10^-2)(0.500) = 6.75 x 10^-3 Wb. Option (c) puts the given 30 degrees straight into the cosine, measuring from the plane - the central angle error of the topic, and one that would make the flux greatest edge-on. Option (a) is B*A, the angle ignored altogether, which is the maximum flux and is obtained only face-on. Option (d) is 40 x 6.75 x 10^-3 = 0.270 Wb, the FLUX LINKAGE of all forty turns where one turn was asked for; N*Phi and Phi carry the same unit, so only reading the question protects you.

questions.q: A coil of 300 turns, each of area 8.0 cm^2, lies with its normal along a uniform field which grows steadily from 0.10 T to 0.90 T in 0.50 s; the total circuit resistance is 6.0 ohm. The magnitude of the induced emf while the field is changing is:
questions.concept: emf = N*A*(dB/dt), with the CHANGE in B and the area converted to m^2
questions.why: A = 8.0 cm^2 = 8.0 x 10^-4 m^2; dB/dt = (0.90 - 0.10)/0.50 = 1.6 T/s; emf = (300)(8.0 x 10^-4)(1.6) = (0.24)(1.6) = 0.38 V. Option (b) is 0.43 V, from using the FINAL field 0.90 T rather than the change 0.80 T - the value of B at the end of the process appears nowhere in Faraday's law. Option (a) is 3.8 kV, from leaving the area in cm^2, a factor of 10^4 and a voltage no such coil could produce. Option (d) is 1.3 mV, with N omitted, which is the emf of a single turn when the turns are in series and their emfs add.

questions.q: The same 300-turn coil (area 8.0 cm^2, resistance 6.0 ohm) now has the same field change from 0.10 T to 0.90 T made TEN TIMES MORE SLOWLY, over 5.0 s. The charge that circulates in the circuit during the change is:
options: 32 mC - the same as before
3.2 mC
320 mC
192 mC
questions.concept: q = N*(change in Phi)/R: the time cancels out
questions.why: The flux change per turn is A*dB = (8.0 x 10^-4)(0.80) = 6.4 x 10^-4 Wb, so q = (300)(6.4 x 10^-4)/6.0 = 0.192/6.0 = 3.2 x 10^-2 C = 32 mC, in the 0.50 s version and in the 5.0 s version alike. Slowing the change divides the emf and the current by ten and multiplies the duration by ten, leaving the product untouched. Option (b) divides by ten as though the charge followed the current - the whole point of the question. Option (c) multiplies by ten, treating the longer time as more charge delivered at the same current. Option (d) is 0.192 C = N*(change in Phi), the flux linkage change quoted as a charge with the division by R forgotten; webers are not coulombs.

questions.q: A straight rod of length 0.50 m is pivoted at one end and rotated at 120 revolutions per minute in a uniform field of 0.20 T parallel to the rotation axis. The emf between its ends is:
questions.concept: A rod rotating about one end gives emf = 0.5*B*L^2*omega, with omega = 2*pi*f in rad/s
questions.why: f = 120 rev/min = 2.0 rev/s, so omega = 2*pi*(2.0) = 12.57 rad/s and emf = 0.5*(0.20)(0.50)^2*(12.57) = 0.5*(0.20)(0.25)(12.57) = 0.31 V. Option (a) is 0.63 V, exactly double: the 0.5 has been dropped, which is the same as using the TIP speed L*omega = 6.28 m/s in B*L*v when the correct speed is the MEAN, 0.5*L*omega. Option (b) is 3.0 V, from putting 120 straight in as omega - revolutions per minute treated as radians per second, an error of 2*pi x 60. Option (d) is 0.050 V, from using f = 2.0 in place of omega = 2*pi*f, an error of 2*pi ~ 6.28.

questions.q: A square loop of side 0.20 m and total resistance 0.50 ohm is pulled at a steady 2.5 m/s out of a region of uniform field B = 0.30 T directed into the page, moving in the plane of the page on a frictionless surface. The force that must be applied to keep it moving at that speed is:
options: zero, since the surface is frictionless
questions.concept: Only the side still inside the field carries current in the field, and F = B*I*L opposes the motion
questions.why: emf = B*L*v = (0.30)(0.20)(2.5) = 0.15 V; I = emf/R = 0.30 A; F = B*I*L = (0.30)(0.30)(0.20) = 1.8 x 10^-2 N, directed back into the field region, so an equal applied force is needed. Check: B^2*L^2*v/R = (0.09)(0.04)(2.5)/0.50 = 0.018 N. Option (a) doubles it by counting a force on the trailing side too, but that side is OUTSIDE the field region where B = 0 and feels nothing. Option (c) uses the loop's PERIMETER 0.80 m as L; the L in B*I*L is the length of conductor lying in the field and carrying current perpendicular to it, here one side only (the two sides parallel to the motion do feel forces, but equal and opposite ones that cancel). Option (d) is the trap the question is built on: 'frictionless' removes mechanical friction and has nothing to do with the magnetic retarding force, which is where the 4.5 x 10^-2 W of heat in the resistor comes from.

questions.q: A coil of 50 turns, each of area 4.0 x 10^-3 m^2, sits in a uniform field of 0.25 T with its normal along the field. It is FLIPPED THROUGH 180 degrees in 0.10 s. The average induced emf is:
options: zero, since the magnitude of the flux is the same before and after
questions.concept: Flipping reverses the SIGN of the flux, so the change is 2*B*A and not B*A
questions.why: Initially Phi = +B*A = (0.25)(4.0 x 10^-3) = 1.0 x 10^-3 Wb; after the flip the normal points against B, so Phi = -1.0 x 10^-3 Wb. The change is 2.0 x 10^-3 Wb, and |emf| = N*(change in Phi)/(change in t) = (50)(2.0 x 10^-3)/0.10 = 1.0 V. Option (a) is 0.50 V, using a change of B*A - the error of thinking the flux merely goes away rather than reversing; it is the correct answer for a 90 degree turn and is wrong here by exactly two. Option (b) is 2.0 x 10^-2 V, with N omitted. Option (d) treats flux as a magnitude with no sign, but Phi = B.A is a signed scalar, and it is precisely that sign change that makes a flipped coil generate twice as much.

questions.q: A coil of 200 turns and area 30 cm^2 is placed in a uniform field of 0.50 T and spun at 40 revolutions per second about an axis that lies ALONG B and in the plane of the coil. The peak emf generated is:
options: zero
questions.concept: No component of B ever threads the coil, so Phi = 0 at every instant and there is no emf at any speed
questions.why: The rotation axis lies along B and in the plane of the coil, so the coil's NORMAL stays perpendicular to B throughout; Phi = B*A*cos(90 degrees) = 0 always, d(Phi)/dt = 0, and the emf is zero however fast it is spun. Option (a) is 75 V = N*B*A*omega with omega = 2*pi*(40) - the generator formula applied without checking the geometry, which is the entire discrimination here; N*B*A*omega is the peak emf only when the coil spins about an axis PERPENDICULAR to B. Option (b) is 12 V, that same misapplication compounded by using f = 40 in place of omega = 2*pi*f. Option (c) is 0.30 V = N*B*A, the rotation rate omitted, which would have a stationary coil generating a voltage.

questions.q: A rod of mass 0.15 kg and length 0.30 m slides on frictionless rails at 4.0 m/s in a field of 0.60 T; the circuit resistance is 1.2 ohm. The driving force is now removed and the rod is left to itself. The total heat eventually produced in the resistance is:
options: indeterminate - the time the rod takes to stop must be known first
questions.concept: All of the kinetic energy ends as heat, because no other sink exists
questions.why: With the driving force removed the only horizontal force is the magnetic retarding force B^2*L^2*v/R, which decelerates the rod exponentially (v = v0*exp(-t/tau) with tau = m*R/(B^2*L^2) = (0.15)(1.2)/[(0.36)(0.09)] = 5.6 s). It never quite stops, but all of its kinetic energy is converted: heat = 0.5*m*v0^2 = 0.5*(0.15)(4.0)^2 = 1.2 J. Option (b) is 0.43 J, the INITIAL power in watts (emf = B*L*v = 0.72 V, I = 0.60 A, P = 0.432 W) quoted as an energy in joules - dimensionally wrong, and in any case the power falls continuously as the rod slows. Option (c) is m*v^2, the factor 0.5 dropped. Option (d) is the answer of someone who intends to integrate I^2*R dt and cannot: the point is that energy conservation gives the total without integrating anything, and does so even though the motion formally never ends.

questions.q: A flat circular coil of 150 turns and radius 6.0 cm is placed in a uniform field with the PLANE of the coil at 30 degrees to the field; the total circuit resistance is 18 ohm. The field is raised steadily from 0.20 T to 0.80 T in 0.25 s. Find (i) the flux through one turn at the start and at the end, (ii) the induced emf and the induced current, (iii) the sense of the induced current, stated relative to the direction of B, and (iv) the charge circulated. Then state what each of your answers becomes if the same rise takes 2.5 s, explain the one that does not change, and say what the emf would have been had the coil been FACE-ON to the field throughout.
questions.concept: Phi = B*A*cos(theta) with the angle from the normal, emf = N*(change in Phi)/(change in t), the direction from Lenz's law, and q = N*(change in Phi)/R independent of the rate
questions.why: Set-up: A = pi*r^2 = pi*(0.060)^2 = 1.131 x 10^-2 m^2. The PLANE is at 30 degrees to B, so the NORMAL is at 60 degrees and cos(theta) = 0.500. (i) Flux per turn: Phi_1 = (0.20)(1.131 x 10^-2)(0.500) = 1.131 x 10^-3 Wb; Phi_2 = (0.80)(1.131 x 10^-2)(0.500) = 4.524 x 10^-3 Wb; the change is 3.393 x 10^-3 Wb. (ii) emf = N*(change in Phi)/(change in t) = (150)(3.393 x 10^-3)/0.25 = 0.509/0.25 = 2.04 V; I = emf/R = 2.04/18 = 0.113 A. (iii) Sense: the flux is INCREASING, so the induced current's own field inside the coil must point AGAINST B. Look along B, so that B goes away from you; the induced field must come towards you, and by the right-hand loop rule (thumb towards you, fingers curl) the current runs ANTICLOCKWISE as you see it - equivalently clockwise viewed from the far side. The mechanical check passes, since whatever is strengthening the field is opposed. (iv) q = N*(change in Phi)/R = 0.509/18 = 2.83 x 10^-2 C (28 mC); cross-check I*t = (0.113)(0.25) = 0.0283 C. Over 2.5 s instead: the emf becomes 0.204 V and the current 1.13 x 10^-2 A, each ten times smaller - but the charge is STILL 28 mC. Why the charge is unchanged: q = the integral of I dt = the integral of (N/R)*(d(Phi)/dt) dt = N*(change in Phi)/R, in which the time cancels identically; a slower change means a proportionally smaller current flowing for a proportionally longer time, so only the total flux change and the resistance matter. That is what makes a ballistic galvanometer possible. Face-on instead: with the normal along B, cos(theta) = 1 and every flux doubles, so the emf would be 4.07 V, the current 0.226 A and the charge 57 mC. The 30 degrees in the question is worth a factor of two, and only because it was read from the plane and had to be converted to 60 degrees from the normal.

questions.q: A square loop of side 0.25 m and total resistance 0.80 ohm travels at a constant 3.0 m/s in the plane of the page, entirely crossing a 1.0 m wide region of uniform field B = 0.40 T directed into the page. Find the emf, the current, the sense of the current and the force on the loop while it is ENTERING, while it is ENTIRELY INSIDE, and while it is LEAVING. Find the heat produced during entry and check it against the work done by the puller over that stage. Then give the total heat for the whole crossing and describe the shape of the emf-time graph.
questions.concept: The emf appears only while an edge crosses the boundary, the direction reverses between entry and exit, and the energy books close
questions.why: While entering: only the leading side sweeps flux, so emf = B*L*v = (0.40)(0.25)(3.0) = 0.30 V and I = emf/R = 0.30/0.80 = 0.375 A. The into-page flux is INCREASING, so the induced field inside the loop must point OUT of the page and the current is ANTICLOCKWISE. The leading side carries that current in the field and feels F = B*I*L = (0.40)(0.375)(0.25) = 3.75 x 10^-2 N directed BACKWARDS, opposing the entry; the two sides parallel to the motion carry equal and opposite forces that cancel, and the trailing side is not yet in the field. While entirely inside: all four sides are in the field, B, A and theta are all constant, so d(Phi)/dt = 0 and emf = 0, I = 0, F = 0 - true even though the loop is moving as fast as ever. This stage lasts while the loop travels 1.0 - 0.25 = 0.75 m, that is 0.25 s. While leaving: the into-page flux is now DECREASING, so the induced field must point INTO the page to maintain it and the current is CLOCKWISE, the reverse of the entry sense; the magnitudes are unchanged at emf = 0.30 V, I = 0.375 A, F = 3.75 x 10^-2 N, again backwards, now pulling the loop back into the region it is leaving. Heat during entry: entry lasts t = L/v = 0.25/3.0 = 8.33 x 10^-2 s, and P = I^2*R = (0.375)^2*(0.80) = 0.1125 W (check emf*I = (0.30)(0.375) = 0.1125 W), so the heat is (0.1125)(8.33 x 10^-2) = 9.4 x 10^-3 J. Check against the work done: the puller supplies 3.75 x 10^-2 N over the 0.25 m of entry, W = (3.75 x 10^-2)(0.25) = 9.4 x 10^-3 J - identical, as conservation of energy requires, since the loop's kinetic energy is constant throughout. Total for the crossing: two identical stages of 9.4 mJ with a free-running gap between them, so the total heat is 1.88 x 10^-2 J and the total work done against the magnetic force is the same 18.8 mJ. The emf-time graph: two rectangular pulses of equal height 0.30 V and equal width 83 ms, of OPPOSITE SIGN, separated by a 0.25 s stretch at exactly zero. The sign reversal is Lenz's law - the loop resists gaining flux on the way in and resists losing it on the way out, and in both cases the force opposes the motion.

questions.q: A coil of 250 turns and area 40 cm^2 sits in a uniform field of 0.30 T, and the total circuit resistance is 12 ohm. (a) It is spun at 20 rev/s about a diameter perpendicular to B: find omega, the peak emf, the r.m.s. emf and the output frequency, and say at which orientation the emf is ZERO. (b) Starting face-on, it is instead FLIPPED THROUGH 180 degrees in 0.040 s: find the average emf and the charge circulated, and explain why the answer is exactly TWICE what a 90 degree turn would give. (c) A rod of length 0.40 m is rotated about one end at the same 20 rev/s in the same field: find its emf and explain the factor by which it differs from B*L*v computed with the speed of the rod's far end.
questions.concept: Peak emf N*B*A*omega for a rotating coil, a flux change of 2*B*A for a flip, and 0.5*B*L^2*omega for a rotating rod
questions.why: Common quantities: A = 40 cm^2 = 4.0 x 10^-3 m^2; N*B*A = (250)(0.30)(4.0 x 10^-3) = 0.300 Wb. (a) The generator: omega = 2*pi*f = 2*pi*(20) = 125.7 rad/s (using f = 20 in place of omega is an error of 2*pi ~ 6.28). Peak emf = N*B*A*omega = (0.300)(125.7) = 37.7 V; r.m.s. emf = 37.7/sqrt(2) = 26.7 V, which is what a meter reads while the peak is what the insulation must withstand; output frequency = 20 Hz, one full sine cycle per revolution. The emf is ZERO when the coil is FACE-ON (plane perpendicular to B), because there the flux is at its maximum and therefore momentarily stationary - the emf follows the SLOPE of the flux, not its size, so it is greatest a quarter-turn later when the coil is edge-on and the flux passes through zero. (b) The flip: face-on, Phi = +B*A per turn = (0.30)(4.0 x 10^-3) = 1.2 x 10^-3 Wb; after the flip the normal points against B, so Phi = -1.2 x 10^-3 Wb and the change is 2*B*A = 2.4 x 10^-3 Wb. emf = N*(change in Phi)/(change in t) = (250)(2.4 x 10^-3)/0.040 = 0.600/0.040 = 15 V, and q = N*(change in Phi)/R = 0.600/12 = 5.0 x 10^-2 C (50 mC). Why exactly twice a 90 degree turn: turning through 90 degrees takes the flux from +B*A to 0, a change of B*A, whereas flipping takes it from +B*A to -B*A, a change of 2*B*A, because the flux does not merely vanish, it REVERSES SIGN. Phi = B.A is a signed scalar whose sign follows the chosen normal, and forgetting that is a clean factor-of-two error rather than a rounding slip. (c) The rotating rod: emf = 0.5*B*L^2*omega = 0.5*(0.30)(0.40)^2*(125.7) = 0.5*(0.30)(0.16)(125.7) = 3.02 V. Using B*L*v with the TIP speed v = L*omega = (0.40)(125.7) = 50.3 m/s gives (0.30)(0.40)(50.3) = 6.03 V, exactly TWICE the correct value. The rod's speed is not uniform: it is zero at the pivot and L*omega at the far end, so each element dr at radius r contributes B*(omega*r)*dr and the integral from 0 to L is 0.5*B*L^2*omega. Equivalently the correct speed to use is the MEAN, 0.5*L*omega = 25.1 m/s, which restores 3.02 V. Any answer that quietly uses the tip speed is asserting that the pivot end moves as fast as the tip.

questions.q: A long solenoid of radius 2.5 cm has 2000 turns per metre, and its current is increasing at 40 A/s. A ring of 30 turns, radius 8.0 cm and resistance 1.5 ohm is placed COAXIALLY AROUND it. Find (i) the rate of change of the field inside the solenoid, (ii) the rate of change of flux through the ring, (iii) the emf and the induced current in the ring, and (iv) the magnitude of the induced electric field at the ring. State the direction of the induced current relative to B. Then explain exactly what a student obtains, and by what factor they are wrong, if they use the RING'S own area instead - and explain why nothing in this problem moves and yet an emf exists.
questions.concept: It is the flux through the ENCLOSED AREA that induces an emf, not the field at the conductor, and the mechanism is the induced electric field
questions.why: (i) Field rate inside the solenoid: B = mu_0*n*I, so dB/dt = mu_0*n*(dI/dt) = (4*pi x 10^-7)(2000)(40) = 0.1005 T/s. (ii) Flux rate through the ring: outside a long solenoid B is essentially zero, so all of the flux the ring encircles is that of the solenoid's own cross-section, A_sol = pi*(0.025)^2 = 1.964 x 10^-3 m^2, giving d(Phi)/dt = (0.1005)(1.964 x 10^-3) = 1.974 x 10^-4 Wb/s per turn. (iii) emf = N*d(Phi)/dt = (30)(1.974 x 10^-4) = 5.92 x 10^-3 V (5.9 mV) and I = emf/R = 5.92 x 10^-3/1.5 = 3.9 x 10^-3 A (3.9 mA). (iv) Induced electric field: for one turn the integral of E.dl round the ring is E*(2*pi*r) = 1.974 x 10^-4 V, so E = 1.974 x 10^-4/(2*pi x 0.080) = 1.974 x 10^-4/0.503 = 3.9 x 10^-4 V/m - and this field exists at radius 8.0 cm whether or not the ring is there, the wire merely giving its charges something to be pushed along. Direction: if B inside the solenoid points UP the axis and is increasing, the induced current must produce flux DOWN the axis inside the ring, so it flows CLOCKWISE seen from above (looking along B, from the end B points towards). The wrong route: a student who uses the RING's own area A_ring = pi*(0.080)^2 = 2.011 x 10^-2 m^2 gets d(Phi)/dt = (0.1005)(2.011 x 10^-2) = 2.021 x 10^-3 Wb/s and emf = (30)(2.021 x 10^-3) = 6.06 x 10^-2 V (61 mV) - too large by the ratio of the areas, (8.0/2.5)^2 = 10.24. The error is to imagine the solenoid's field filling the whole disc bounded by the ring, when it is confined to the 2.5 cm-radius core and is essentially zero over the remaining 97 per cent of that disc; multiplying a field by an area it does not occupy is the commonest way to get a flux wrong. Why there is an emf with nothing moving: Faraday's law contains only d(Phi)/dt, and motion is one way of producing it, not a requirement. Here the solenoid current rises, so B rises, so the flux through the ring's enclosed area rises, and an emf follows. Microscopically the changing flux creates a circulating ELECTRIC field in the surrounding space (the integral of E.dl = -d(Phi)/dt), and it is that field, not any magnetic force on moving charges, that drives the ring's current - exactly how a transformer works, and why 'there must be relative motion between the coil and the field' is wrong.

checks.topic: Applied design judgement on decomposition and software design: judging the cohesion of a module you are shown and the coupling of a supplied code fragment or interface sketch, spotting a decomposition that is modular in name only, choosing the better of two supplied designs and saying exactly what makes it better, reading a structure sketch to name horizontal or vertical partitioning and its named cost, deciding which of the two design approaches a described situation calls for, and telling a refactoring from a change of external behaviour

questions.q: A team takes one 5,000-line file and splits it into ten files of 500 lines each. Every file still reads and writes the same set of global variables, exactly as before. What has been achieved?
options: Modularisation, since the program's functionality is now divided into ten separate modules saved in separate files, which is the course's definition

A separation into files but not into modules: the definition requires independent modules each holding everything it needs, and ten units sharing one set of globals still cannot be changed without affecting each other - meanwhile all five disadvantages have been paid
High cohesion but high coupling, since each file is now small enough to have a single aim while the shared globals keep the files dependent on one another
A refactoring that will need to be reversed, since the course lists longer compilation and loading time as a disadvantage and no advantage has been gained to offset it
questions.concept: Modularisation divides functionality into independent modules; splitting files divides text
questions.why: The definition requires independent modules, each with everything it needs to implement only a part of the functionality. Ten units that all read and write one set of globals are not independent: any of them can be affected by any other, so the stated benefit - being able to make changes to different parts of our code without affecting other parts - has not been obtained, and the fault the deck complained of, changing a part of the code can affect other parts of the code, is untouched. Meanwhile the disadvantages have all arrived: more units to compile and load, more inter-module communication, more design time spent. Option a treats 'saved in separate files' as the definition; the deck offers that as something modularisation permits, not as what it is. Option c is the most tempting wrong answer and fails on cohesion: file size has nothing to do with whether the functions in a unit serve one aim, and slicing a 5,000-line file every 500 lines will cut straight through aims rather than between them. Option d misuses 'refactoring': nothing here is defined by unchanged external behaviour, and the deck lists the compilation cost as a disadvantage to be accepted, not a reason to reverse a design.

options: A, because the rate is held in one place instead of being repeated at every call, which is what avoids duplication in a design
A, because B has two parameters where A has one, and a narrower interface is by definition the more loosely coupled of the two

B, because net_pay no longer depends on config existing, on the name SETTINGS, or on three levels of key nesting - the rate can still be held in exactly one place, and what B removes is payroll's knowledge of where and how it is stored
B, because a function with no imports executes faster, and the course lists execution time among the disadvantages that a good design must minimise
questions.concept: Coupling is what a module must know about another, and information hiding removes the possibility of knowing it
questions.why: Design A's net_pay cannot perform its function until it knows that a module called config exists, that it holds a name SETTINGS, that SETTINGS is a nested structure, and that the rate lives under the keys 'tax', 'paye', 'rate' in that order. Every one of those is a data structure or processing detail of another module, which is exactly what information hiding says must not be accessible; rename one key and net_pay breaks. Design B depends on nothing - the caller supplies the rate, so the rate may still be held in config and read once, at the edge of the system, by the module whose aim that is. Option a is the strongest distractor because its premise is true and its conclusion does not follow: B does not duplicate the rate. The rate stays in one place; what moves is the knowledge of where that place is. Option b counts parameters as though a shorter signature were automatically looser; A's true interface is not one parameter but one parameter plus an entire nested structure it silently reads, and a hidden dependency is worse than a declared one precisely because the header does not warn you. Option d reaches for a real item from the disadvantages list and applies it as though design were an optimisation exercise; execution time is not the ground on which coupling is judged.

questions.q: A module named 'user_utils' contains hash_password, resize_avatar, send_sms and parse_csv_export. None of the four calls any of the others. Judge it.
options: High cohesion, because none of the four calls another, so nothing inside the module depends on anything else inside it
Low coupling and therefore high cohesion, since the two always move together and a module with no internal dependencies is by definition well formed

Low cohesion: the module has no single ultimate aim for the four functions to work towards, and the deck's own example is exactly this - a component performing four functions with a limited relationship with one another, to be refactored into four components each with high cohesion
Cohesion cannot be judged from this information, because cohesion is a measure of how often functions call one another and no call frequencies have been given
questions.concept: Cohesion asks whether the functions serve one ultimate aim; it is not the inverse of coupling and it is not about internal calls
questions.why: Password hashing, image resizing, SMS sending and CSV parsing are four aims. There is no sentence of the form 'this module's ultimate aim is ...' that all four serve, which is precisely the deck's refactoring example - a component performs four functions that have a limited relationship with one another, to be refactored into four different components, each exhibiting high cohesion. The name 'utils' is the usual signature of the fault. Option a inverts the test outright: absence of internal calls is neither evidence for nor against cohesion, since two functions serving one aim need not call each other. Option b is the trap the whole item is built for, and the single most common misuse of the vocabulary: it treats cohesion and coupling as one measurement, so that improving one must improve the other. They are readings taken in different places - coupling between modules, cohesion inside one - and this module demonstrates the point by scoring badly on cohesion while saying nothing at all about coupling. Option d states a definition of cohesion the course does not give; the course's is the ultimate aim of the module, which is fully judgeable from the four names.

questions.q:
Two versions of the same module's published interface. Which follows information hiding, and what specifically does it buy?

# VERSION A                          # VERSION B
class Account:                       class Account:
    balance = 0.0                        def balance(self): ...
    entries = []                         def deposit(self, amount): ...
    overdraft = 0.0                      def statement(self): ...
options: A, because it exposes three items where B exposes three functions, and exposing data is cheaper than exposing behaviour, so less crosses the interface

B: the data structures are not accessible to other modules, so 'entries' can become a database table and 'overdraft' a computed rule without any other module changing - which is the stated benefit that changes in one component are restricted from affecting others
A, because a caller of A can read balance without a function call, so A is more loosely coupled: fewer calls between modules is what low coupling means
Neither, because information hiding concerns whether other people can read the module's source, and both versions are equally readable
questions.concept: An interface that exposes data structures cannot hide them, and what hiding buys is freedom to change
questions.why: Version A publishes three data structures - a float, a list and a float - so every other module may read them, and some will. From that moment 'entries' must remain a list, 'balance' must remain a stored number rather than a computed one, and 'overdraft' must keep its name. Version A therefore makes the deck's third benefit unavailable: changes in one component are no longer restricted from affecting others. Version B publishes only what the module does, so 'entries' can move to a database table and 'balance' can become a computation over the entries, and no other module changes a line. Option a argues that exposing data is cheaper; it is cheaper to write and far more expensive to change, and the quantity crossing the interface is not the measure - what the other side may depend on is. Option c is the persistent 'coupling means call traffic' error in its most seductive form: reading account.balance looks like less interaction than calling account.balance(), but it is more dependence, because it fixes how the value is stored as well as what it is. Option d is Week 8's misreading of hiding as secrecy, restated at module scale; both versions are equally readable by a person, and only one of them is unreachable by other code.

questions.q:
Read this structure. Which partitioning is it, and what are the two kinds of module called?

                    admissions_controller
                    (chooses which operation to run; almost no computation)
                   /            |             \
        read_form()      score_applicant()      print_offer()
        (all input)      (all computation)      (all output)
options: Horizontal partitioning, because a control module is present and control modules are what horizontal partitioning uses to communicate between functions and execute them

Vertical partitioning: the functionality is distributed top-down, with a control module at the top performing the decision-making and doing little processing, and worker modules below performing all input, computation and output
Horizontal partitioning, because the three lower boxes sit side by side across the diagram rather than one beneath the other
Neither, since structural partitioning applies only where the architectural style is not hierarchical, and this structure is plainly a hierarchy
questions.concept: Vertical partitioning distributes functionality top-down into control and worker modules
questions.why: The deck's sentence matches the sketch word for word: the functionality is distributed among the modules in a top-down manner; the modules at the top level called control modules perform the decision-making and do little processing, whereas the modules at the low level called worker modules perform all input, computation and output tasks. The controller chooses; the three below it do the reading, the computing and the printing. Option a is the trap, and a fair one: control modules are mentioned under horizontal partitioning too - control modules are used to communicate between functions and execute the functions - so the presence of a controller decides nothing. What decides it is that the split here is by level of responsibility (deciding above, doing below), not by function side by side. Option c reads the geometry of the drawing rather than the structure: any hierarchy drawn on paper puts siblings side by side, and horizontal partitioning means one branch per major function, each branch containing its own deciding and doing. Option d inverts the precondition - the deck introduces structural partitioning precisely for the case where the architectural style of a design follows a hierarchical nature.

questions.q: A designer is asked to refactor a module that fetches, totals and renders a report. She splits it into three modules, and while doing so notices that the total was including a cancelled order and corrects it. Has she refactored?
options: Yes - the split improved the internal structure and correcting an obvious error is part of improving a design, since the deck says the existing design is checked for flaws during refactoring
Yes, and the fix is what makes it a refactoring: a change that leaves a known bug in place has not improved the module's behaviour or function
No, and the split was the mistake: refactoring reduces the complexity of module design, and going from one module to three increases it

Not purely: the split is a refactoring because external behaviour is unchanged, but the corrected total changes what the system outputs for the same input, so that part is a behaviour change and must be a separate step - otherwise, if anything breaks, nobody can say which of the two changes did it
questions.concept: Refactoring is defined by unchanged external behaviour, which is why a behaviour change must not be mixed into one
questions.why: The split leaves outputs identical, so it is a refactoring - modifying a software system to improve the internal structure of design without changing its external behaviour. The corrected total does not: for the same input the system now prints a different number, which is a change of external behaviour and therefore, by definition, not part of the refactoring. The practical reason to keep them apart is the whole value of the word: a refactoring carries the guarantee that nothing observable changed, so if a test fails afterwards, something is wrong with the restructuring. Merge a deliberate behaviour change into it and that guarantee is gone - a failure could now be the split or the fix, and the two must be untangled by hand. Option a misreads 'the existing design is checked for any type of flaws like redundancy, poorly constructed algorithms and data structures': those are design flaws - structure - not incorrect outputs, and correcting them is what leaves behaviour unchanged. Option b inverts the definition, making behaviour change a requirement of refactoring, which would leave no word for the thing that changes structure safely. Option c misreads 'reduces the complexity of module design' as 'reduces the number of modules'; the deck's own example goes from one component to four and calls that a reduction in complexity, because complexity is measured per module design, not per count.

questions.q: 'orders' calls 'stock' in fourteen places. Told to reduce coupling, the team merges the two into one module, 'sales'. The coupling between 'orders' and 'stock' is now zero. What has actually happened?
options: The coupling has genuinely been removed, since coupling is the extent to which modules depend on other modules and there is no longer another module for either half to depend on

The coupling reading fell to zero because the boundary was deleted, not the dependency: the same code still needs the same information, but it now runs where no interface governs it - and cohesion has fallen, since 'sales' now has two responsibilities
Coupling has fallen and cohesion has risen, since the fourteen call sites are now internal, and functions that call one another inside a module are exactly what high cohesion means
Nothing has changed either way, because coupling and cohesion are properties of the functionality, and the same functionality is present before and after
questions.concept: Coupling is a reading taken across a boundary; deleting the boundary deletes the reading, not the dependency
questions.why: Nothing about what the code needs has changed - the same fourteen places still require the same stock information at the same moments. What has changed is that they now run inside one module, where no interface constrains them, no review sees them, and nothing prevents them growing into reads of each other's internal structures. And the merge costs cohesion: 'sales' now carries two responsibilities, so the single responsibility principle - modules should not have more than a single responsibility - is broken to satisfy a coupling metric. The correct operation is the reverse: keep the boundary and narrow what crosses it. Option a is exactly the reasoning the team used and is why this is the week's most misunderstood idea: it treats the metric as the goal, and any two coupled modules can be 'fixed' by merging until the whole program is one module with a coupling of zero - the very 5,000-line function the deck opened by condemning. Option c misuses cohesion as 'the functions call each other a lot'; the test is one ultimate aim, and 'sales' now has two. Option d is right that the functionality is unchanged and wrong that nothing has changed: cohesion and coupling are properties of the division, which is precisely what was altered.

questions.q: A department already owns a tested library of working modules - student_record, fee_ledger, course_catalogue - and now wants a results portal built from them. Which approach does the course say suits this, and why?
options: Top-down, because the portal is a new system that does not yet exist, and top-down is the approach used whenever a system is being designed
Top-down, because the portal's requirements are known in full, and top-down is the approach used when the specific details of a solution are already known

Bottom-up, because the approach starts from the most specific and basic components and composes higher-level components from them, and is more suitable when a system is created from an existing system whose basic primitives can be used in the newer one
Bottom-up, because the portal is a small system, and top-down is reserved for systems large enough to need more than one level of decomposition
questions.concept: Bottom-up suits building on existing primitives; top-down suits designing from scratch when details are unknown
questions.why: The course states it directly: the bottom-up design model starts with the most specific and basic components, proceeds with composing higher level of components by using basic or lower level components, and is more suitable when a system needs to be created from some existing system, where the basic primitives can be used in the newer system. Three tested modules are exactly such primitives. Option a comes from remembering only that top-down means 'start with the whole system', and treats newness as the criterion; the criterion the course gives is whether the specific details are unknown, and here they are known - the modules exist and their interfaces can be read. Option b inverts the course's own condition: top-down is more suitable when specific details are unknown, not when they are known. Option d invents a size rule; neither approach is described in terms of system size, and the deck insists that a good combination of both is used at any size - the portal's top-level structure will still be decided top-down, and the two meet in the middle.

questions.q:
This module works. Name every thing it depends on inside 'results', say exactly which of them are hidden data structures that should not have been accessible, state what happens on the day 'results' moves its rows into a database, and rewrite it. Then say which of the two possible rewrites gives both modules better cohesion, and why.

# module: transcript
import results

def gpa(student_id):
    rows = results.TABLE
    mine = [r for r in rows if r[0] == student_id]
    return sum(r[2] * r[3] for r in mine) / sum(r[3] for r in mine)
    # column 0 = student id, column 2 = grade point, column 3 = credit units
questions.concept: Naming a hidden dependency exactly, and repairing it so that each module keeps its own aim

questions.q: A component 'Registration' contains validate_input, create_account, send_confirmation_email and compress_profile_photo. Judge its cohesion and say precisely on what grounds. Apply the deck's refactoring, showing what you end up with, and state the payoff the deck claims for it. Then answer the harder half: a colleague, seeing this succeed, proposes splitting a genuinely high-cohesion module 'fee_ledger' (post_charge, post_payment, balance, statement) into four modules by the same reasoning. Say what happens to cohesion and coupling if he does, and what that shows about when splitting is the right operation.
questions.concept: Judging cohesion, applying the deck's refactoring, and recognising when splitting is the wrong operation
questions.why: 'Registration' has low cohesion. The test is whether the functions work together to achieve the ultimate aim of the module, and there is no single aim these four share: validating input is a rule-checking job, creating an account is a storage job, sending an email is a messaging job, and compressing a photo is an image-processing job. Note the ground carefully - it is not that the four are never used together. They may well all run during one registration, and a student who answers 'high cohesion, because they all happen at sign-up' has confused being invoked in the same sequence with serving the same aim. The evidence for four aims is that each function would change for a different reason: a new password rule, a new database, a new mail provider, a new image format. The refactoring is the deck's own example - a design model might yield a component which exhibits low cohesion, like a component that performs four functions that have a limited relationship with one another, and software designers may decide to refactor the component into four different components, each exhibiting high cohesion. So: Validation -> validate_input; Accounts -> create_account; Notifications -> send_confirmation_email; Media -> compress_profile_photo; plus a thin Registration that calls the four in order, with the same inputs and the same outputs as before. The deck's claimed payoff is that this leads to easier integration, testing, and maintenance of the software components - and it is a refactoring only because external behaviour is unchanged. The harder half: post_charge, post_payment, balance and statement all serve one ultimate aim - maintaining and reporting a student's financial position - and all four operate on the same ledger entries. Split them into four modules and two things go wrong at once. Cohesion falls rather than rises, because each new module holds a fragment of one aim rather than the whole of a smaller aim, so none of them can be described without mentioning the other three and none satisfies 'has everything it needs to implement only a part of the functionality'. Coupling rises sharply, because the ledger entries must now live somewhere reachable from all four, so either they become shared data - the fault of the ten-files question - or three modules must call the fourth on every operation, which is a boundary crossed on every posting. The five disadvantages arrive too: more inter-module communication, more calls at run time, more design effort, for no benefit. What this shows is that splitting is not a general improvement; it is the correct operation only where the seams already exist. The deck splits a component because it exhibited low cohesion - because it already contained four aims and merely lacked the boundaries between them. Cutting along a seam raises cohesion and adds almost no coupling; cutting across one lowers cohesion and adds a great deal. The question to ask before splitting is therefore not 'is this module big?' but 'can I name two aims in it, each of which would change for a different reason?'

questions.q:
Two designs for a results system are proposed.

DESIGN 1 - one module per technical activity
    validation      validates students, results, fees, staff records
    database        every read and write in the system
    email           every message the system sends

DESIGN 2 - one module per area of the business
    student_records  holds student data; validates and stores it; answers questions about it
    results          holds results; validates and stores them; computes GPA
    notifications    sends whatever it is asked to send

Choose one, and justify the choice in the week's own terms - cohesion, coupling, information hiding, and the single responsibility principle. Say what happens under each design when the rule for a valid matriculation number changes, and what happens when the database is replaced. Then name one of the course's five disadvantages of modularisation that you incur either way, and say why it is worth paying.
questions.concept: Choosing between two decompositions, and judging the choice by change
questions.why: The choice is Design 2. Cohesion: in Design 2 each module has a nameable ultimate aim - student data, results, notification - and every function in it serves that aim. In Design 1 the module 'validation' has no single aim at all: it validates students and results and fees and staff records, four unrelated bodies of rules that change for four unrelated reasons. 'database' is worse, since 'every read and write in the system' is not an aim but an activity, describable only by listing everything the system does. Design 1's modules are 'utils' modules with respectable names. Coupling: in Design 1 no feature lives in one module, so student-record functionality is spread across validation, database and email and every one of those must know the shape of a student record - three modules depending on one structure. In Design 2 the structure of a student record is known to 'student_records' and to nothing else. Information hiding: Design 2 permits it, since how student data is stored is a processing detail inside 'student_records' and the other modules pass only that much information as is required. Design 1 forbids it, because 'database' must know the internal shape of every kind of record in the system in order to store it - the data structures are accessible everywhere by construction. Single responsibility: Design 2's modules have one responsibility each; Design 1's have as many as the system has kinds of data. Under a new matriculation-number rule, Design 2 changes one module, 'student_records', and nothing else compiles differently; Design 1 changes 'validation', which also holds the rules for results, fees and staff, so the change is made in a module four unrelated features depend on, and a mistake there can break any of them - the deck's original complaint verbatim, that changing a part of the code affects other parts of the code. When the database is replaced, Design 1 looks better at first sight - one module to rewrite - and this is the honest half of the answer. But 'database' must still be rewritten for every kind of record it holds, so the work is the same; the difference is that in Design 2 the change is made three times in three modules that can be changed and tested independently and by different people, which is the first stated advantage of modularisation, while in Design 1 it is one large simultaneous change to a module the whole system depends on. A disadvantage incurred either way: most obviously that inter-module communication problems may be increased, since every request that used to be a local call is now a crossing between modules with an interface to agree, keep stable and get wrong; or that modularisation demands more initial design time, since deciding where the boundaries go produces no running code on the first day. It is worth paying because the alternative is the 5,000-line function the deck opens with: cheap to start and unchangeable thereafter. The cost is paid once, at the start, in design; the benefit is collected at every change for the life of the system.

questions.q:
Read this structure, name the partitioning, and say which of the course's named costs it carries.

   fees_controller  <->  results_controller  <->  transcript_controller
        |                      |                        |
   compute_fees()        compute_gpa()            format_pdf()

Then redraw it under the other kind of structural partitioning, naming the modules and saying what each does. Finally, say which of the two structures makes it easier to add a fourth feature, and which of the course's stated benefits of structural partitioning that illustrates.
questions.concept: Reading a structure, naming the partitioning, and knowing which cost belongs to it
questions.why:
The partitioning is horizontal. The system is divided into three side-by-side branches, one per major function - fees, results, transcripts - each with its own control module, and the control modules communicate between the functions and execute the functions, which is the deck's description of horizontal partitioning. The deciding and the doing are not separated by level here: each branch decides and computes within itself. The named cost belongs to horizontal partitioning specifically: it requires the passing of more data across the module interface, which makes the control flow of the problem more complex, especially where data moves rapidly from one function to another. The double arrows in the sketch are that cost made visible - a transcript needs results, results need fees to be cleared, so data crosses between the three controllers constantly, and the path a single request takes through the system is no longer readable from any one branch. Redrawn vertically:

                    portal_controller          <- CONTROL module: decides which
                    (decision-making only;        operation runs; little processing
                     almost no computation)
              /              |               \
   read_request()      compute()          render_output()
   (all input)      (all computation)     (all output)   <- WORKER modules

Here the functionality is distributed top-down: one control module at the top performs the decision-making and does little processing, and the worker modules below perform all input, computation and output tasks. Whether a request concerns fees, results or a transcript is now a decision taken in one place rather than a conversation between three peers, and the data crossing interfaces is the single request travelling down and the single result travelling up. Which makes a fourth feature easier: the horizontal structure does, and this is the point worth having. Adding a fourth feature means adding a fourth branch beside the other three, and the three existing branches need not be opened at all.
